speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: INCREASE IN DOMESTIC PRICE TO SI .55 PER BUSHEL PLUS CARRYING CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make at this time with regard to wheat policy. In doing so I am speaking for my colleague the Minister of Finance as well as for myself, and I am also referring to matters that come more particularly under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of Agriculture.
As an important element in price control, the government, through the wartime prices and trade board, has maintained maximum prices for wheat products milled and sold in Canada for human consumption. This programme has been in effect since August 1, 1942.
These ceiling prices, very important from the standpoint of living costs during and since the war, could only be maintained if wheat were provided to processors on the basis of prices existing in the base period in the fall of 1941. It was established that the highest cash price of western wheat during the base period was 77| cents per bushel for No. 1 northern wheat in store Fort William-Port Arthur. Effective on August 1, 1942, when the board's fixed initial price was increased to 90 cents per bushel, the government provided for a drawback to be paid to mills and other processors of wheat for consumption in Canada. This drawback was the equivalent of the difference between the basic price of 77$ cents per bushel and the monthly average price for western wheat. Since September, 1943, the drawback has been based upon the difference between 77| cents per bushel and the prevailing domestic price of $1.25 per bushel.
On September 27, 1943, trading was suspended on the Winnipeg futures market and the government, through the Canadian wheat board, took over all unsold stocks of wheat in commercial positions. This wheat became the property of the government with no further producer interest. These crown stocks, amounting to nearly 300 million bushels, were then used for mutual aid purposes and wheat for the domestic market. They were disposed of at approximately the prices at which they were acquired. These crown stocks lasted until January, 1945. In acquiring additional supplies of wheat for mutual aid purposes early in 1945 the government paid the board's current com-
Labour Conditions

mercial price, which was SI .46 per bushel, less an allowance for carrying charges. At that time, however, the government felt that over-all price control in Canada required the establishment of a domestic wheat price. Consequently the Canadian wheat board was directed to make wheat available for domestic consumption at 81.25 per bushel which was the fixed initial price being paid to western producers. The government continued to absorb carrying charges on domestic wheat and continued the drawback to processors to maintain the basic price of 77$ cents per bushel. This arrangement has continued up to the persent time.
This part of price control has involved the expenditure of public funds. Drawbacks paid to processors of wheat products sold in Canada have for the past three years, been running at the rate of $18,000,000 to $20,000,000 per year. Under the system in effect since August 1, 1943, millers and other manufacturers of wheat products have been required to refund all drawback which would have put them into the excess profits category.
The field of price control in Canada is being progressively narrowed and the government is of the opinion that the Canadian wheat board should no longer be required to sell wheat for domestic consumption at $125 per bushel. Accordingly the government has decided that Wheat shall be sold for domestic consumption on the same basis as provided in the United Kingdom contract. The government has therefore directed the Canadian wheat board to advance the domestic price of wheat to $1.55 per bushel plus carrying charges. This direction is effective at once.
I wish to state explicitly that prevailing ceiling prices on flour, bread, mill feeds and other wheat products are not affected by this change in the board's selling price of wheat for domestic consumption. The government, through the treasury, will continue as in the past to make wheat available to millers and other processors at prices appropriate to these ceilings. The government regards this continuation of price ceilings on flour, bread and other wheat products as a necessaiy part of its programme of orderly decontrol.
The feed wheat subsidy of 25 cents per bushel is being continued, but the increase in price to $1.55 per bushel plus carrying charges will mean an increase of slightly over 30 cents per bushel in wheat used for feed in Canada. Because of the continued overseas demand for wheat for human food, the government feels that as far as possible grains other than wheat should be used for feed purposes in this country.

I should like also to announce at this time that the Canadian wheat board is today establishing open delivery quotas for oats and barley, effective immediately for the remainder of the crop year.

subtopic: COAL MINERS' STRIKE IN THE MARITIME PROVINCES
COAL MINERS' STRIKE IN THE MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will no doubt wish to have a statement from me in connection with the conference which was held on Saturday between representatives of the United Mine Workers of America and the collieries operated by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited, Nova Scotia, over which I presided.
I regret to say that it was not possible at that conference, to find a basis of compromise between the conflicting positions of the parties.
It will be recollected that in the latter part of January I appointed the Hon. Mr. Justice W. F. Carroll, of the supreme court of Nova Scotia, a commissioner to deal with the dispute and that the commissioner's report was laid on the table of the house on February 13.
Following conferences between the parties held in Ottawa in January, in which I and officials of my department participated, the original demands of the union were reduced to three; namely, (a) a wage increase of $1.40 per shift; (b) 8 cents per ton on coal produced for the establishment of a welfare fund; (c) a 5 per cent contribution by the company on payroll to a pension fund which would also be contributed to by the employees concerned.
Prior to this, the company had made a proposal to the union that it would increase wages to a maximum of $1 per shift on the basis of an increase in production, the increase in wages to be on a graduated scale until the pre-war levels of production had been reached, at which point the maximum increase in wages of $1 would be payable.

Penitentiaries
The recommendation of the commissioner was that the increase in wages asked for by the men was justified and that there was also justification for the establishment of welfare and pension funds.
In dealing with the wage recommendation, however, the commissioner approved the proposal of the company as to the graduated increase of SI per shift based on production, the additional 40 cents to make up the total of SI.40 per shift, to be obtained by other means.
Basically, the conflict between the company and the union is one of principle. The company's position is that it cannot agree to any increase in the wage rate except on the basis of increased production. The union states that production is wholly a managerial problem and one over which the individual miners or the union have no control.
It was admitted at the conference on Saturday that the absentee problem in the collieries owned by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation was a serious one and the union representatives were willing to agree to a provision in a new contract which would obligate it to deal cooperatively and effectively with that problem as well as with the problem of production.
Production figures supplied to me recently by the office of the government coal administrator, for Dosco and associated companies, show a serious falling off in production per man days since 1939. These figures are as

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMISSIONER-ADMINISTRATION OF PENITENTIARIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMISSIONER-ADMINISTRATION OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to lay on the table the report of General R. B. Gibson, commissioner appointed under Order in Council P.C. 1313 of April 5, 1946, to make an inquiry into and recommendations regarding the penitentiaries system of Canada.
I believe I should refer to one passage in the report, which is as follows:
The government has recently decided that for the present it is preferable to entrust the administration of the penitentiaries of Canada to a single commissioner assisted by two deputy commissioners, with a headquarters organization consisting of the inspectors and staff of the present penitentiaries branch, the inspectors being reclassified as assistant commissioners.
I should say that General Gibson did not feel he should be asked, and indeed he was not asked, to make any recommendation on the point as to whether the Archambault report should be varied in that respect. That is the decision of the government, however, which has been arrived at for reasons which we regard as good, and which will be given to the house when penitentiaries legislation is introduced later this session.

These three questions refer to the disposition of small items or office equipment that have been handled by War Assets Corporation. There is no objection to giving this information if we have it, but there are two practical difficulties. One is that it is impossible to prepare an answer accurately, the second is the very great cost of preparation. The following difficulties have been presented to me by War Assets Corporation:
(a)	War Assets Corporation does not maintain a record of original costs.
(b)	As a result of the introduction of the decentralization of sales policy, all records of sales to individual firms are maintained in the region and branch sales offices.
(e) Prior to November, 1945, declarations of surplus covering miscellaneous items of equipment sometimes including office furniture were received by the corporation. These would have to be checked to separate office furniture from other equipment.
(d)	When the information referred to in paragraphs (b) and (c) had been found, it would then be necessary to check against the invoices to ascertain the purchaser.
(e)	The only alternative would be to extract the required information from copies of invoices available in the market research and statistics division at head office which would involve a listing of information from some 4,000 or 5,000 invoices, many of which would not be broken down to show individual prices for individual types of equipment and many others of which show only office furniture and equipment with no description.
, (f) Custodian sales and sales of plants including land, buildings and equipment invariably include items of office furniture and equipment, a record of which is not kept under the office equipment classification.
. (g) To compile the information required, not including a list of equipment sold on a custodian sales basis, would cost at least $4,000 to $5,000, and would take twenty full time employees at least a month to prepare it. The finished report would probably run to a list of around a hundred pages.
It would be possible, however, to give the bulk return received on sales for any given period for "office furniture and equipment", not including furniture and equipment forming part of sales of complete plants. This return would include desks, chairs, tables, business machines and all types of office equipment such as cellulose tape, binders, etc. This return could be further broken down showing total sales to distribution centres, that is, the province to which the equipment was shipped and the total sales made to the dominion government.
I trust that under the circumstances hon. members will decide for themselves whether the three questions are worth $5,000 to the recipients. I suggest that in the meantime, if hon. members are not willing to allow them to drop, the questions stand for further consideration.

HIS MAJESTY'S ABSENCE IN SOUTH AFRICA- COUNCIL OF STATE
speechtext:
,1. Does the council of state appointed to exercise regal functions during His Majesty's absence from the United Kingdom in South Africa, have any authority in respect of Canada?
2.	If so, what is the nature of that authority?
3.	Was the Canadian government consulted regarding the appointment of this council of state?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The answer is no, but perhaps I should add this word of explanation.
On January 17 the governor general informed the Prime Minister, through his secretary, of the arrangements which had been made in the United Kingdom for a council of state. He said that during the King's absence, the Duke of Gloucester, the Princess Royal, and Lord Lascelles, would be appointed counsellors of state, with powers, restricted by the terms of the letters patent to certain subjects, to act for His Majesty within the United Kingdom. He added that, throughout his tour, the king would continue to transact as usual any business submitted to him by his ministers in Canada.
The action which has been taken in the appointment of the present council of state is provided for by the Regency Act, 1937, which enables counsellors of state to be appointed to carry out necessary royal functions in the United Kingdom during the king's absence. The act has no application to Canada, and the counsellors of state have no jurisdiction in respect of Canada.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, February 14, consideration in committee of Bill No. 14, to amend the Militia Act-Mr. Clax-ton-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Friday night it was considering section 19.
On section 19-Cadet corps command.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I believe I raised this question the other day in the house for the first time. I wish to add something to what I said then with respect to the action taken.
I am afraid the minister does not understand the principles on which the cadet system was started in Ontario with education. It is unfortunate that at the present time there is no minister in the government from the Toronto district, and that the present minister and the parliamentary assistant came from one province. Neither of them came from Ontario where the greatest activity in the militia is found in cadet work.
Cadet corps were set up shortly in Ontario after confederation-because at that time we were part of the British empire; it seems now, however, that every day we are being talked out of it. I say we are not going to be talked out of the British empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire. I am getting sick and tired of hearing hon. members make such statements, forgetting we are still part of that empire. Let me say to the minister that, with all due respect to him, he was never a public school cadet as one thinks of cadets in Ontario under this bill. My understanding is that he was a fine cadet officer in a corps in Lower Canada College, a private school. I have great respect for him and for his parliamentary assistant. I am ready to admit that he was a soldier in the first world war and that, as I have said, he did serve in a cadet corps in a private school.
We know that shortly after confederation the cadet system was set up under boards of education, comprising public and separate school boards throughout the country. But now the minister is going to upset the whole thing; with one wave of his hand he wipes out cadets fourteen years of age and under. Let me say to him that we came through two long wars through the aid of that cad'et system.
In the old days, in my native city of Toronto I began my public life serving on a school board; and the backbone of the militia and of recruiting in Ontario from the time before the Fenian raids, down through the South African war and the northwest rebellion, and through the two great wars, was the cadet system. In Ontario, after confederation, it did magnificent work, and the other provinces were glad to copy what had been done in that province. That was the system which developed after the Ryerson school bill.
Now what does the minister propose? He proposes to upset the whole thing and practically to wipe out all cadet public school corps of boys under fourteen years, the boys who have been the backbone of the cadet system. There are very few boys left of fourteen years in our public and separate schools in Ontario because today under a new system they have reached the first and second forms of high school at that age, and have moved up.
Today the minister proposes to upset that policy. Let me tell him that if he does that he will destroy the whole militia system. Now training is to be given two or three nights in the week. The school principals are complaining about this. These boys should be receiving cadet training in the public and separate schools. I might add that the De La Salle high school also has a fine cadet corps. But instead of permitting the departments of education to handle cadet training the minister is upsetting all that and making it federal.
The cadet corps which up to now have been operating in schools have had the advantage of training by men who have returned from service in two wars, and who have been prepared to give their time free. The boys have become so well trained in Toronto that on
Militia Act

many occasions they have won rifle shooting championships of all Canada. If the minister proceeds with his plan he is going to upset all this, and he will destroy the very foundation of the militia system as it was established in 1877.
Another feature to be considered is that the cadet developed a respect for authority. He was improved physically and in many other ways and became a credit to the school system. They, their children and their children's children have performed a worth-while service, and if the system is abolished the backbone of the militia of Canada has been destroyed.
A few nights ago a meeting of the board of education in Toronto was held. I am afraid they did not know this bill or are not familiar with the situation here because they say they believe the move being made by the minister was solely one in the interests of economy. It is not only an economic move, it is an abolitionist move. These outside cadet corps will interfere with the boys' studies in the schools. How can they keep up with the activities carried on in the high schools today? They cannot afford to go out a couple of cadet nights a week and miss their studies.
The same activities are carried on during school hours by the school boards. Uniforms are supplied and the government is relieved of all expense. It seems as though a great many people are afraid to mention the word "empire" but they are not afraid of that word in the United States. New York state is known as the empire state, and then there is the commonwealth of Massachusetts. The whole cadet system is based on flag and empire. We have Empire day on May 23 when the cadets in the different schools used to hold a big parade on University avenue, Toronto, and showed splendid training and ability in drill and all that kind of thing. Among the schools in Toronto there is keen competition as to which has the best cadet corps, Dufferin, Wellesley or Ryerson of old. As I say these cadet corps are the militia background of the whole system. At last Thursday's board meeting Doctor Goldring, the superintendent, said he could get little news of this bill from the newspapers.
So far as I am concerned we might just as well meet here in secret. The public back home do not know what is going on re abolition of cadets. I was asked many questions at a meeting in my constituency on Friday night. The people wanted to know what was going on here and they said they never saw it in the newspapers. In olden days we had six newspapers. I am not here to criticize the press-far from it; I have found

them a fine, decent lot, and I have had a great deal of experience with them. I can tell you that you cannot argue with any newspaper
because they always have the last word.
The people at this meeting on Friday night wanted to know if the cadets were to be abolished over the heads of the municipalities and the school boards. I could not inform them what goes on here in just five minutes. Patriotism has been abolished, especially in our history books. Prime Minister Attlee of Great Britain has stated that we do not owe any allegiance to our country; the new international part is the supreme part. He tells us to forget about our country because we have an international order. Patriotism is the cement that binds nations together. As Macaulay says, "history is patriotism teaching through example". All that has been abolished. Instead of love of country being developed we are being told that our goal now is an international order. As I say, patriotism is the cement that binds nations together, but instead of teaching Green's "History of England" in the schools, our boys and girls are told that our goal now is an international order. To such follies have we come that education has now lost its grip on common sense and the moral and political standards and on life.
The school boards in Ontario have not been consulted about this bill and they know nothing about it. The cadet system in the schools has cost the government little money. Wait until we see it next year under the new corps. Instead of having to spend two nights a week away from their studies, these boys should be learning how to qualify for positions in business and all that kind of thing. I feel quite sure that the department of education of Ontario no matter what we do, will continue the cadet system in the public schools.
There is one school in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for St. Paul's, which has a cadet corps numbering 640 enlistments in the last war, and about eighty-three of those cadets were killed in the last war. The same thing will be found in all the schools in Toronto. Education is a matter of property and, civil rights and belongs to the provinces. My. hon. friends come from Quebec, a very fine province, but I think they are going a little too far in trying to upset the Ontario school cadet system.
Why not let this stand over for a year? The time has come when we should hearken to the handwriting on the wall because this is going to lead to disruption in the schools.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Friday evening we had just reached section

Militia Act
19, which deals with cadet corps command, drill and equipment, et cetera. I do not desire unduly to take up the time of the committee, but I feel that this is a matter which should be thoroughly discussed and not passed over lightly. Hon. members will agree that the training of our youth, whether it be scholastically, culturally, artistically, practically or whatever else it may be, is training which lasts. When we are speaking of the cadet corps we are speaking of a training which lasts.
As I see it, cadet corps as they are set up in Nova Scotia or British Columbia or anywhere in between are set up on six basic principles. In the first place, it is felt that the cadet corps and service in the corps will generate a sense of national pride and conscience as few other media will. Service in a cadet corps will give to the young lad the idea of "My Country" as will few other equivalent means. In the first place, he wears the king's uniform, which in itself is a challenge, not only for its traditions but for what it means.
We have been altogether too lax in this country, diversified as wTe are with new citizens, to impress upon our people the idea of "My Country". If we turn our eyes to the south we will see in the United States of America, highly diversified as it is and has been, a melting-pot which offers a challenge faced by no other country. They have the salute to their flag in their schools and they repeat, the oath of allegiance every morning. This is done for one reason and one reason only, to build up the idea of "My Country". So it seems to me that through the cadet corps in our schools there can be given to the young lads in the fullest and best possible way the idea of "My Country", in other words, a sense of national pride and conscience.
Then, second, what better way is there of developing in the young lad a sense of selfconfidence, a feeling that he is somebody, that he is not just another person but that he has his responsibility? He is part of a precision machine, composed not of mechanical parts; he is not an automaton but an individual, working in the closest possible harmony with his fellows, and the discipline and the training that he gets through that means instils into him a sense of self-confidence which those of us who have passed through the cadet corps know full well.
In the third place, it tends to foster leadership and to generate within the young lad that sense of leadership which in wide degree varies from one to another but is latent in all. Those of us who have watched the cadet corps and seen them in action have again and again seen a young lad who has been just
another student in the school suddenly rise to leadership and assume proportions of which he himself never before suspected himself capable. He gets a chance of promotion to corporal, sergeant, staff-sergeant. He can do something, and tangibly.
In the fourth place, what better means is there of producing physical fitness among our young men? It was shocking at the start of this last war, as I have often mentioned in this house and only just recently, to learn of the lack of physical fitness of the Canadian eighteen years of age and older so far as military service was concerned, and that is the test. In the cadet corps the lad has a chance in his earliest days to gain a physical fitness which he would not otherwise get.
In the fifth place, it can supply a highly beneficial outlet for the natural energy and restless activity which are characteristic of all youth. One has only to look over the postwar record of world war I to realize how great a wave not only of crime but of juvenile delinquency swept this and other countries. One hesitates to say that history is repeating itself, but even thus early after world war II the same thing is being noted to a degree at least. What better way is there of keeping a lad usefully and, from his own point of view, profitably occupied than to give him an outlet for his physical energies through the cadet corps? I have not the figures nor could I get them before this afternoon, but from such experience as I have had, which is considerable, I would hazard the guess that the number of juvenile delinquents whose names are on the muster roll of a cadet corps is very small.
Lastly, it provides elementary training of a practical nature in case of a national emergency. As some one said recently in this house, we prepared for world war I as we did for the Boer war, and we prepared for world war II as we did for world war I. That is axiomatic in our military history. We have always banked on the time element to allow us to develop a new fighting force subsequently to the declaration of war. Can we, dare we forget that the time element which has always played into our hand will never again play into our hand? The technical and scientific nature of modern warfare is such that there will not be time to raise an army, navy or air force after the first gun has been fired or the first bomb has been dropped. The lifeblood of our three services is the young men who today enrol in the cadet service. We hope to God that their services will never actually be required in war, but surely
Militia Act

we think enough of them and of the homes they will establish to make it safe for them to plan those homes.
What is the present position in regard to the cadet corps? Section 10 of this bill reads:
Sections sixty, and sixty-one of the said act are repealed and the following substituted therefor:-
"60. Each cadet corps shall be subject to the authority and under the command of such officer as may be appointed by the minister."
"61. Cadet corps shall be drilled and trained as prescribed by the minister and may be furnished with arms, ammunition and equipment under conditions prescribed by him."
I asked the minister this question in the house on February 12, which appears at page 351 of Hansard:
Will he-
That is the minister.
[DOT]-be prepared to make a statement within the next day or so in regard to the fate he has in mind for the sea, army and air cadets.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) replied:
... It seems to me that the question of the cadets, reserves and active forces can properly be dealt with when the estimates are reached. I could deal with those matters, if the house wished, at some length on the orders of the day, but I do submit that would not be a proper use of the orders of the day.
I asked, Mr. Chairman, about the confusion relative to the future of cadet corps that existed across Canada and I wish to say to the minister, in spite of his answer to me on the orders of the day on Wednesday last, that there is confusion. What is the future of the cadet corps to be? If it is generally understood, or presumed, that there are to be no sponsored cadet corps in the primary schools, what support is -there to be for the cadet corps in the secondary schools? Whether the minister phrases it as seventy-five per cent of the requirements as stated last year or as a twenty-five per cent cut in the three services, the fact remains that the three armed services are to be only seventy-five per cent of what was originally planned for post-war. What is the fate of the cadet corps on this basis? Here we are in 1947, just a little over a year and a half away from V-J day. It seems to me that history is repeating itself even thus early. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has already referred this afternoon to the primary school cadets. We remember them, both before, during and immediately after world war I. What happened to them? There stood up in this chamber one member after another who, no doubt sincerely-who is to question that?-but under the spell of the pacifism that was then sweeping over the world, thought it was unneces-

sary for us to have this show of militarism in Canada, so that they beat about and badgered the government of the day until it succumbed and the primary school cadets virtually disappeared. That was the aftermath of world war I. Can it be that we are heading the same way again? Is history repeating itself? Can we never learn a lesson? Are we, just eighteen or nineteen months after V-J day, facing again the fact that the guts are being tom out of the cadet corps of Canada?
We have the sea cadets, a most excellent organization, an organization which made to the war a glorious contribution of which Canada will ever be proud, sponsored by the Navy League of Canada, and they have done a magnificent piece of work. We have the army cadets which contributed magnificently in their own way, virtually on their own, without such a benefactor as the navy league of the sea cadets. The hon. member for Broadview referred to one school in Toronto, out of whose cadet corps-a primary school, mark you-over 600 lads enlisted in the armed forces and of whom sixty-two did not return; they paid the supreme sacrifice. They received a grant of $4.25 a year from the government in Ottawa.
Then there are the air cadets. I can speak with some personal feeling in regard to the air cadets, for it was my privilege to have a good deal to do with their inception, called as I was from my station in December, 1940, to report to air force headquarters in regard to their organization. I saw it at first hand and had at least some small part in the development of the air cadets and the Air League of Canada.
The air cadet league has made an outstanding contribution. These lads, in so far as they have had the chance, have come through and showed the stuff of which they were made, and in their own way they made a contribution to the Royal Canadian Air Force second to none.
What is the position with regard to these three groups, the sea cadets, the army cadets and the air cadets? There are three separate acts to control their 'activities. Without burdening the committee with the acts, I shall let it rest there. There are three separate acts to control their activities, but if you shake it all down it will be found that in very great part the success of the cadets, whether it be sea, army or air, is due to the local organization, to the local people through the league in the case of the navy, through the league in the case of the air, through wellmeaning citizens or upstanding high school principles or whatever they may be, in the case of the army. And they have done a job.

Militia Act
But where is the federal authority? True, the armed forces themselves, the navy, the army and the air force, through their personnel, through their equipment, through their training syllabi, and by other means, have contributed most generously and successfully. But from what I have said, hon. members will imagine that there is a national result across Canada which shows a highly diversified outcome; for the simple reason that if the local organization, wherever it may be, is good, then the cadets are good; if it is mediocre somewhere else, then the cadets are mediocre; if it is poor somewhere else, then the cadets are poor. Why should that be? Simply because there is a lack of a central control, a central coordinating body, which surely is the federal authority.
What is offered to the sea cadet? Not only does he get excellent training in the normal course of events, but if he distinguishes himself and proves worthy he has a chance to go to sea in the summer time. What about the air cadet? The air cadet has a chance to go to an airfield in the summer time, to get a few flips, to hold the stick and see how it feels, to get instructions for a fortnight from the instructors at the particular station who are fully qualified to give it. But what about the army cadet?-and it is for him that I speak particularly. The army today is "full up"-to use his own words-with gadgets which are fascinating to him. The new armaments appeal to him enormously. What he would give to go to some army post somewhere, some station somewhere or a camp where, for example, there are tanks to be driven, to be told about tanks, to learn about tanks. Why should not he have the same relative opportunity as the sea or air cadet?
The whole thing is out of balance, and yet if one surveys the numbers enrolled, without laying them before the committee, he will find that the number of sea cadets is relatively small, the number of air cadets is relatively small, the number of army cadets is large compared with the other two, but all three are woefully small compared with the youth and young man population of the Dominion of Canada. The great outcry is not alone for the continuance of the cadet system; it is not only for a continuance but for a bolstering of it, a building of it up, a levelling off of the cadet system between the three services, sea, army and air at a new high level.
There are those who will argue, as apparently the minister does, that the cadet corps have no place in primary schools. Well, I take issue with that, and grave issue. The school to which I made reference and to which
the hon. member for Broadview made reference is a primary school, and what a contribution it has made. I have under my hand a letter from its principal which I shall not take the time to read into the record; but it is a record of achievement of which he should be proud. Let hon. members realize that in 1945, out of every ten lads in Canada who completed the eighth grade, only seven went on to the ninth. In other words, if you take the cadet corps out of the primary schools, then you are depriving three lads out of every ten of getting cadet corps training, and to me, frankly, that does not make sense.
Take the small country schools which give not only the primary but the secondary courses. There are comparatively few pupils in many of these schools, but there are enough boys in the whole school to make a cracking good cadet corps; there are not enough seniors to make a cadet corps; therefore there is no cadet corps at all because there is no training provided for those in the primary courses.
For those who feel that that corps training may be too military, that there may be too much emphasis placed upon the military end of it, let them remember that the effect of th\>
military training goes to the senior boys. The junior boys are not mentally prepared or equipped to accept the sort of training which the older boy is. Therefore if you remove the cadet corps from the primary grade, then you are asking your cadet corps to become more and more military. I merely state, this in passing.
I should like to make these suggestions to the minister.
In the first place, I feel that there should be a centralization of control for the combined services. In recent weeks we have witnessed the bringing together into one building under one minister of the chiefs of staff of the three services, something which is acceptable to them, certainly acceptable to the minister and, I think, acceptable to hon. members. It is a good move, as the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out the other day with such outstanding eloquence and clarity, and as was also pointed out by the hon. member for Trinity. You cannot take a country from the air. The army must march in; the army cannot get there unless the navy takes it there, and both the army and the navy need umbrellas. All three services have to work together. Never has there been such a coordinated team as there was in world war II. Therefore we set up a cadet corps for the navy, for the army and for the air force, so that Tom, Dick or Harry does not know what the other one is
Militia Act

doing. It does not make sense. There should be a coordination of effort of the cadet corps under one combined/ command in Ottawa. If it is necessary for the three armed forces, it is equally necessary for the cadet corps.
Second, there should be a central cadet organization in Ottawa, which, after all, is the headquarters of our three armed services. Again, let us recognize that the problems of education are the problems of the individual provinces, and that there is always danger of treading upon provincial autonomy or of domination by the dominion. For the moment let us not get into such things in connection with the matter I am discussing. They have their place and, as I pointed out before, the autonomy of a province is a precious thing. It is precious to me as a resident of one particular province. But we are now talking about a Canadian service, all-embracing as far as Canada is concerned. I do not suggest that there should be abridgment of autonomy or domination from Ottawa in these matters, but direction; and the purpose of that direction would be unquestionably to raise the standard of performance of all cadets, and to equalize the national effort.
Why should it be that the cadet corps in one place is better than the cadet corps in another? If it is dependent solely upon the local authority to do what it can here, what it can there, that is bound to be the case. But why should it be that this or that province cannot compete interprovincially because they have not the same opportunity in one province as in another? That does not make sense either.
I think the minister will realize that there is a certain amount of friendly competition among the three services. The navy knows it is the senior service and governs itself accordingly. God bless it. The army knows that, where it may be on paper junior to the navy, it is certainly senior to the air force. We admit we are the junior service, the youngest most virile and the best of all. That competition is there. But put that sort of feeling into the hearts and minds of youngsters and it ceases to be competition and becomes rivalry. That is the sort of thing you do not want to inculcate in youngsters.
Imagine little Mr. Sea Cadet seeing little Mr. Army Cadet going off for the summer to drill on the drill square while he is going off on a ship; and imagine little Mr. Air Cadet seeing little Mr. Army Cadet going to the drill square when he is going off to fly! But let the army cadet be able to say, "Fly if you want to; I am going to drive a tank".

I say, equalize the opportunities which the lads will have and then build up interprovincially; build up your inter-command, interdistrict, whatever it is, and you will not have any question of rivalry. You will have competition.
In the third place, I would suggest to the minister that he rewrite all three acts into one. Make it one act to be known as the Cadet Act of Canada. Let us away with pigeon-holing the navy or the army or the air force. Instead, bring them all into one act. There can be sufficient flexibility to meet the three services.
In the fourth place, let there be equality of schedules and syllabi as laid down by each service and directed by the central authority. Let there not be any one corps as a whole, a national corps, in any one service better than the others except by proven worth rather than by equipment given or chances afforded:
In the fifth place, broaden the training for all these cadets. Do not limit it to whatever it may be that can be done within the confines of the school building or the schoolyard. Let the army take on its responsibility in connection with these lads in the fullest possible way. Show them what a route march
is,	what it is to bivouac, what it is to use the latest mechanical devices, and all the rest of
it.	And the same with your air force, your air cadets, and your sea cadets. Broaden the training in all three services.
In the sixth place, let there not be any appointment of officers by someone far removed from the local scene. Take only the navy league, which appoints the officers for the sea cadets, and I am quite sure that the hon. member for Wentworth, who has himself proven so efficient in that capacity, will bear me out when I say that that system works. Let the local authority under the league do the appointing of officers.
Lastly, let there be a close liaison between the leagues, navy, army and air force, and the senior naval, army or air officer commanding. Let them work together for these ends and not vie with one another to see who can raise the most money locally to get this or that which is better than can be got somewhere else. Let us all work together.
Now let me look back for a moment at section 19. I can see the purport of Bill No. 14. We, on this side of the house, have endeavoured to point out what we felt to be its weaknesses; but as far as section 19 is concerned, I think it is insidiously and woefully dangerous and is farther reaching than perhaps the minister realizes. If he realized

Militia Act
just how far-reaching it is I am sure he would have none of it. It makes the minister a sort of supemational chief boy scout. He is the Pooh-Bah of Canada's military youth. I point out to him that that particular section is the ward heeler's delight. The minister, a civilian, elected to parliament, a member of a party, becomes a member of the government and is going to take into his hands the appointment of cadet officers.

I am not saying; I am not suggesting or even insinuating that there has been, and I am not suggesting that under the present minister there will be. But this bill, I repeat, is not written for today. I am looking ahead a little bit, and it is one of those things that can creep in and prove at a later date to be the most destructive, violent and vicious instrument. Frankly, I do not see the point of it at all. I am visualizing what may happen, and it seems to me that this sort of thing is the method-to use an extreme example-that Hitler used to produce a generation which this world has grown to loathe and to hate, for the simple reason that when once politics-inadvertently or otherwise-creeps into this type of set-up, then, to use the language of the services, "you've had it".
So I point out to the minister, as earnestly as I can, where that section may lead, and I make it clear to him, as to the former secretary of state who interrupted me, that I am casting no aspersions on the minister. I am
pointing out the danger of that section being on the statute books of the country, and accordingly I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), an amendment to this section, with the following recommendations:
1.	That there be cadet training in the primary schools of Canada.
2.	That there be centralization of cadet direction as there is at present in the armed forces.
3.	That there be broadened and brightened syllabi and activities in all three cadet services.
4.	That there be greatly increased grants to all three cadet services to accomplish these purposes.
5.	That this may be the case, and I repeat what I said in the beginning, in order that within our youth there may be generated a national pride and conscience, so that selfconfidence may be developed, together with a sense of leadership and ambition, with the promotion of physical fitness, and at the same time an outlet be supplied for the unbounded energy and restless activities of our boys, by means of this elementary military training.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo, that section 10 of Bill 14 be deleted.

I think just about everything that can be said has been said about this section, but I should like to say a word in connection with cadet training in the primary schools as reported at page 414 of Hansard the minister said:
... we will bring the army cadet training into line with that for the navy and air force, and limit the training to the boys who can benefit from it. Those are boys between fourteen and eighteen years of age.
The minister refers to the boys who can benefit from this training. I wish to point out to him that in my own city of Toronto cadet training has been of the greatest benefit, not particularly to those boys over fourteen years of age but to the younger boys. They start in at ten, eleven, twelve or thirteen years of age, and in some of the schools where we have a good many so-called new Canadians, or Canadians of middle European descent, it has given these boys a sense of being Canadians. That is where you have to start; the early stages is the time to train these boys. Two or three times here the Jesse Ketchum school in Toronto, under Mr. Kirk, has been mentioned. Of the boys who attended that school, 640 went to the war and over sixty were killed. Cadet training has been maintained in that school since those boys were ten, eleven or twelve years of age, and it has had wonderful results. There is groat need
Militia Act

in other parts of the city for the same thing. I do not know the cost of training these boys under fourteen years of age; I do not think it would be very great, but I believe the training has been a wonderful thing for the underprivileged boys, of whom I have many in my own riding, because most of them never have an opportunity to go to high school. They begin to work at an early age; they have only a very short time to be in the cadet corps; so why should they not have the opportunity to receive this training? It does not do them any harm, and it gives them much greater pride in their own schools than they would otherwise have. The mere fact that they wear the little red coats of which they are all so proud gives them greater incentive to be good Canadians.
The decision to train these boys only where there are groups of twenty or more is a factor of some importance outside the larger cities. Look at the number of schools throughout the country which will be deprived of this training because they will have fewer than twenty boys over fourteen years of age.
I do not want to take up more time, but I did wish to register my protest against the decision of the minister, or the decision of somebody else, to cease military training in the schools for boys under the age of fourteen. Those who have told him that the greatest benefit will be derived by boys over fourteen years of age do not know what they are talking about. The younger they are when they get this training, the better.

the principal has always found the discipline and educational standing of the school have been greatly improved.

I find myself very much in the position stated a few moments ago by the hon. member for St. Paul's, in that I believe nearly everything that can be said on this subject has been said this afternoon; and since I am always critical of repetition in this house, I shall be brief.
I should like, however, to mention one angle of this matter. I am not so much concerned with the military, naval or air training that the youth in the cadet corps of this country are to receive; I am concerned with the character building and discipline that create a better youth in the properly conducted cadet corps. I know, from personal experience in connection with naval and sea cadets, that where at one time we had juvenile delinquency to a considerable degree, through the efforts of the chief of police who was instrumental in helping bring about the organization of a good sea cadet corps in the community, today we have practically no juvenile delinquency. In addition to that, many of the lads who are passing out of the sea cadet corps are better equipped in every way to make a good showing in life. Many of these boys who might otherwise have been directed to a life of crime have been greatly helped.
In my opinion, the cadet movement in Canada should not be curtailed in any way, not only from the point of view of a training ground for members of the armed forces, but from that of character building and disciplinary training which the youth of our country get at a time when they will go in one direction or another, toward becoming either good citizens or criminals.
If it follows from section 19, as has been suggested this afternoon, that the minister will have authority to appoint all commanding officers of cadet corps in Canada, then all I have to say is that our cadet system is being thrown into the laps of local politicians.

In respect of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood, might I point out that in my opinion it is a negative motion, and the defeating of the motion to carry this clause would have the same effect.
The hon. member's motion is that section 19 of the bill be deleted. I would refer the committee to standing order 76, which states:
In proceedings in committee of the whole house upon bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order; the preamble and title to be last considered.
Then paragraph 669 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, states:
Each clause is a distinct question and must be separately discussed.
And paragraph 676 states:
An amendment which would produce the same result as if the original motion were simply negatived is out of order.
It occurs to me that to negative the motion to adopt section 19 would have the same result as the hon. member's motion. Therefore I rule the amendment out of order.

Thus far I have not taken part in the debate on Bill No. 14, in the belief that matters before the house should be dealt with by those who are familiar with them. Not having been a military man, I have refrained up to now from taking part in the discussion. However, I hold a somewhat different position in this discussion concerning cadets because I was associated' with the cadet movement for a number of years. Even now, through my connection with the Navy League of Canada I have something to do at least with making preparations for the training of sea cadets. So that when any matter pertaining to cadet training comes before the house, I feel I should say at least a few words. I shall be brief, however, because up to now the matter has been well handled by the hon. members for Broadview, Greenwood, St. Paul's and Wentworth, the last named within my knowledge having had considerable association with sea cadet training.
I am frankly alarmed as to the portent of the discussion in respect of cadets. For many years, and particularly between 1930 and 1940,
many bitter attacks were made in this house upon cadet training. During those years I had the pleasure

and I always considered it such-of rising in defence of that training.
I remember clearly that one hon. member, who is not now in the house but who represented at that time the constituency then known as Southeast Grey, was most bitter in her attacks on cadet training. Fortunately, however, to the house came a distinguished lady from the constituency of Yukon, who had had wide experience in cadet training because of her sons' having taken cadet courses, following which they performed outstanding, service in the first great war. When the then hon. member for Yukon was finished with the hon. member for Southeast Grey on that occasion I do not believe we heard anything further from the hon. member for Southeast Grey against cadet training.
As I listened to the debate today, I asked myself this question:	Must we go over once
again this performance of debating cadet training? I cannot add much to what has been said by other hon. members, but from my long association with cadet training I know tha-t. what they said is true. I agreed particularly with the hon. member for Greenwood when he pointed out that, better than any other type of training to which young people are subjected, cadet training teaches them to be good citizens, to be civil, courteous, manly and smart in their actions. I have always supported this type of training, and have opposed any measures taken against it.
I fear that at some time a minister who might not be as friendly to cadet training as the present one might hold office, and if the whole programme were beyond the control of local authorities it would be too bad for this country.
In my own city of Toronto there is the Oak-wood collegiate institute which has an excellent cadet corps. On many occasions I have wratched these boys training in the schoolyard, and it has been a delight to me to see them performing the evolutions they were called upon to perform as cadets, and1 how smartly they went through their drill. I am glad to know that the cadets of that school won the rifle-shooting contest. I am not sure whether it was for the whole of Canada, but in any event it covered a very wide field.
I rose merely to add my voice to what has been said on this side of the house in protest against any move that will restrict our cadet training. On the contrary, I will support any programme brought into this house by this or any other government, if I am in the house
Militia Act

when another government comes in, to promote greater and wider cadet training. As I said when I rose, and as I say again, nothing will do as much for the young folk as a thorough, sound and efficient system of cadet training.

I appreciate the words of the hon. member for Davenport and I agree with him. I agree with some of the opinions that have been offered this afternoon, but I would point out that section 19 is an all-important section. One thing we found out in this war was that we needed the coordination of the various armed services and that we needed standardization of arms and equipment. Who can give this better than the minister or the officers appointed by the minister under the new section 60, which will read:
Each cadet corps shall be subject to the authority and under the command of such officer as may be appointed by the minister.
What could be more necessary than that if we are to try to coordinate our efforts? I am a great believer in the cadet corps because I once was a member myself. I think they are a splendid institution, both for building up morale and patriotism and also for providing military training for the youth of Canada. But this training must be coordinated and it must have some definite direction. It is all very well to say that that direction could come from the officers appointed by town councils or other bodies, but I maintain that you could never get standardization or bring about coordination along general lines no matter how well intentioned the people making the appointments might be or how well intentioned the officers who were appointed might be.
This is most necessary if we are to look upon our cadet corps as a possible future fighting force, which, after all, is what it should be if the need should ever arise. Therefore we must have definite direction through parliament, which means through the Minister of National Defence and down the line to the officers commanding who are appointed by the Minister of National Defence. The new section 61 will read:
Cadet corps shall be drilled and trained as prescribed by the minister and may be furnished with arms, ammunition and equipment under conditions prescribed by him.
I am thoroughly in agreement with that. I think anyone who realized how difficult it was during the war, even in the N.P.A.M., to get sufficient ammunition and one thing and another will also agree. If you have the minister coordinating the whole effort you will [Mr. MacNicol.l
have a far better opportunity of supplying your cadet corps with the necessary equipment and other facilities than if you have the disjointed) effort which is bound to occur if each town or city is allowed to appoint the commanding officer.
I do not wish to take up more time with this section, but I could not let it go by without expressing my views because I sincerely feel that I am right. I hope that section 19 of Bill No. 14 will pass without too much debate or criticism.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I would point out one thing to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare who has just spoken. We are not suggesting that the officers commanding the cadet corps would be appointed by the cities or' towns or villages. The present section 60 reads:
All cadet corps shall be subject to the authority and under the orders of the district officer commanding.
There is no suggestion there that a town could appoint the cadet officers. My view is that what has been said by the hon. member for Greenwood is sound. Not only is the present section better than the one the government proposes to substitute, but there should be no change in it until the whole question of the coordination of the cadets in the three services is considered and dealt with. I would much rather see the cadet corps under the command of the district officers commanding than under any other command. I am sure that the officer actually supervising the cadets in any command must be a soldier. I do not think it is fair to an officer commanding a command to have a soldier junior to him running around his command issuing orders and not being responsible to the officer commanding the command. I think the minister would be well advised to take what has been said on this side of the house under consideration and agree that this section shall not be amended1 until he has had an opportunity of reviewing the whole situation.

Has the government or the minister received any complaints from the school commissionaires association of Quebec in connection with the training of the cadet corps in the schools? Would the minister give the committee a statement on the methods that are used for the recruiting of cadet corps?
Mr. PEA.RKES: One of the great objections we have is that the control of the cadet corps

is placed under the minister instead of being under the district officer commanding. The result is that these various cadet corps could easily become political footballs. Since the previous amendment has been ruled out of order, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood:
That section 19 be amended by deleting the words, "such officer as may be appointed by the minister" in line 40 and substituting therefor the words, "the officer commanding the command in which the cadet corps is located," and deleting the words, "by the minister" in line 42 and the words, "by him" in line 44.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the subject of the cadets in Canada, I should like to join with those who have already spoken in recognizing the importance of the work of the cadets, in either the navy, the army or the air force. I feel that those who have spoken critically have said what they did because they have not understood the position, and because of that it might be useful if I put on Hansard a summary of the situation regarding cadets in Canada at the present time.
In the first place, it should be said that cadet work in Canada goes back a long time, and that the cadets have been a useful instrument not only in youth development, as has been stated by other members, and in building up a better .physique and in giving a sense of comradeship, of unity, and of service to the country, but also as a training ground for those who might enter the reserve or active forces of Canada. They have done good work, and nothing we intend will interfere with that work. But the feeling of the officers is, and I must say that since I have looked into it I share their opinion, that while there has been exceptionally good work done in connection with the cadets in Canada there has been some wasted effort, and it is believed that the cadet forces of Canada can be made more useful if the service is limited to boys between the ages of fourteen and eighteen who are capable of availing themselves of the training. This does not mean at all that I do not think that boys below the age of fourteen should not receive training of various kinds; but it does mean that the officers of the department take the view, and I share it, that boys below fourteen years of age should not receive military training in this country at this time, and that the training which they
should get can better be given by other agencies which do not come under the scope of the federal government.

speechtext: It is mutual. I was going to ask the minister, who has said that he has consulted the military authorities and has been given their opinion, did he also consult the headmasters and principals of schools and teachers?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I have consulted some headmasters and some teachers; I have had some experience myself, not only as a cadet, but also on the board of a school, and I must say that, as a result of my experience, I am in accord with the views of the officers. With the greatly improved training facilities of every kind which we now have, we believe that the cadet work for boys between the ages of fourteen and eighteen can be made very much more valuable to the country and very much more interesting to them, and that it should also lead a considerable proportion of those boys into the reserve forces after they have graduated from the cadets.
May I give the committee a brief description of the situation regarding cadets before, during and after the war in the navy, army and air force? May I say at once that what is intended in consequence of these proposals is not a curtailment of cadet work to anything like the pre-war level. Hon. members will see, when the estimates are brought down, that they envisage an expenditure on cadet work fifteen times as great as the amount expended on cadet work before the war, but the expenditures will not be as great as the peak reached during the war years. Our belief is that we should not continue to make expenditures on military purposes at anything like the peak during the war years, but that we should go forward to a post-war arrangement which will meet the needs of the country both with regard to the active and reserve forces, as well as the cadet forces, and do it in a way which will give the utmost value for the taxpayer's dollar expended on defence.
We may look at the situation regarding the navy first. Prior to the end of 1941, the sea cadet movement was comprised of some twenty-five units, totalling 2,500 cadets and
Militia Act

was entirely operated by the Navy League of Canada as an army cadet corps. Training grants and part of camp costs were paid by the army. At the end of 1941 the navy assumed responsibility for this support. During the war the number of sea cadets expanded to some ninety corps, totalling at the peak about
15.000.	Prior to and during the war, drills were carried out two nights a week, if possible.
At present there are 12,000 sea cadets enrolled, of whom about 7,000 are in active attendance. Raising the age limit from twelve to fourteen will lead to the total enrolled number dropping to about 10,000, which is the top figure which it is felt can be effectively handled at present.
A new progressive training syllabus has been issued, drawn up on a basis of one two-hour parade a week, to be augmented by as many voluntary parades as possible. In addition, in those towns and cities in which naval divisions are located-in some twelve out of eighteen places where sea cadets are established-more advanced courses are being held for the more advanced and older cadets. The training year culminates with the summer camps, which this year have been allowed for on a basis of 4,000 cadets for a seven.day period or a longer period for a smaller number.
Let us look at the army. Before the war there were 70,000 army cadets, a considerable proportion of whom were under fourteen years of age. Camps were not generally provided during the immediate pre-war years. During the war the total strength reached a peak of
114.000.	'
At present there are 91,000 cadets, of whom about 50,000 are estimated to be between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. Following the end of the present school year, army cadet training will be organized in two types of corps: (a) open corps affiliated with reserve force units, and so forth; (b) school corps sponsored by boards of education, some of which are also affiliated with reserve units. Altogether 344 corps are affiliated and further affiliation is being strongly encouraged.
Terms of enrolment are, in open corps, ages fourteen to eighteen years; and in school corps, students enrolled in grade 9 and under eighteen years of age at September 1, 1947.
A strength of twenty cadets will be required to form a corps. It is expected that a quota of 50,000 will take care of all the present senior cadets. A new improved programme of training is to be issued. Camps of seven days will be available for eight thousand boys with generally one camp for each command. General officers commanding will have author-

ity to increase the number of days at camp up to a maximum of ten days for a fewer number of boys.
With regard to air cadets, there were no air cadets before the war. They were started in 1940 and reached a peak of 32,500 cadets in 360 squadrons. The training during the war was 100 hours a year plus fifteen days in summer camp for about 10,000 boys.
The post-war target for the air cadets is
15,000	in 225 squadrons. The present strength is about 15,000 senior cadets. I may say that the air cadet league have agreed that that is about the right number for air cadets and have settled on the allocation. The peacetime training provides for eighty-six hours annually for all with an additional fifty-five hours of practical instruction during fifteen days at summer camps which are provided this year for 6,000 cadets.
In each case the totals of boys in age groups fourteen to eighteen, who are expected to be in active attendance and available for training, will be within the totals mentioned for this year's work. While quotas have been allotted to the various commands, these are intended as a guide for purpose of planning and will be subject to adjustment as circumstances require.
I repeat, post-war training will be greatly superior to that before the war with regard to trained instructors, training facilities, clothing, equipment, weapons and so forth.
I have given this summary picture of the situation regarding cadets, and believe that it does meet every point made with regard to cadets by hon. members who have spoken in this discussion or have criticized what has been proposed outside the house, except the one question of junior cadets. On that I say our view is that it is preferable not to give boys under fourteen years of age military training at this time, and if they are to have physical education, group work or other kinds of activities to arouse their interest in their country, to give them opportunities for organized work and development, then we believe that that training should be done by some agency other than the federal government.
May I now touch on some of the questions raised by hon. members? The hon. member for Greenwood referred to the fact that in the United States they salute the flag and had, as he said, a great demonstration of patriotism. I must say that I have a great respect for our good neighbour to the south; but, despite the measures adopted, I do not believe that we need to take second place to them or to any other country in the patriot-

Militia Act
ism of our youth in Canada. He mentioned the fact of juvenile delinquency, which is frequently raised in this connection. I understand that juvenile delinquency is less today than it has been for a good many years; and I would suggest that while group work is undoubtedly a useful way of preventing juvenile delinquency, that work can best be carried on below the age of fourteen by agencies other than the federal government.
The hon. member referred to the fact that he thought our cadet work as between the navy, army and air force was out of balance. That is arguable, possibly, at the present time. This year we propose to have 50,000 senior cadets in the army, 10.000 in the navy and
15.000	in the air force. What other division should be made, I do not know. That seems to be a good one, in view of past experience. It is not out of all proportion to the armed forces, and it does take account of the fact that there are, we believe, enough local agencies interested to take care of that number of boys and to do it well, though possibly not in full this year.
The hon. member urged that there should be a centralization of the control of cadet work with regard to army, navy and air cadets. If by that he means the closest possible coordination so as to ensure similarity of training, in so far as the training can be similar, similar syllabi and similar terms and conditions, then I am in complete agreement with him. This is being worked through the interservice committees of the officers of the three services engaged in cadet work; but I would point out that his very suggestion cuts directly across the amendment first proposed by himself and then the succeeding amendment put forward by the hon. member for Nanaimo who wants to leave the control of army cadets under the general officer commanding the command, and not have that degree of coordination which, I submit, can come only through their heading up at Ottawa in whoever happens at present to be the one person who is responsible for all three services, namely the minister himeslf. This suggestion of the hon. member for Greenwood and the suggestion made by the hon. member for Nanaimo would be directly counter to the second and third objects in the list enumerated by the hon. member for Greenwood and would avoid that coordination and degree of directed activity which we are aiming to have. The fact is that this proposal made by section 19 is expressly and deliberately intended to recognize the increased importance which we attach to cadet corps work. We believe that, in
order to bring that work to its greatest possible development in Canada, it should be directed from defence headquarters at Ottawa.

speechtext: By the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The hon. member can say "by the minister", but under our parliamentary system the minister is responsible for everything that goes on in the department. As the hon. member probably knows, the minister does not personally deal with matters of command of individual corps. What the section says is that each cadet corps shall be subject to the authority and under the command of such officer as may be appointed by the minister. The minister in this case would invariably act on the recommendation of the district officer commanding the command. The general officer commanding the command would have to send his recommendation in to the minister, where it would be recommended to and approved in the same way as are appointments, promotions and retirements, by the governor in council. All these are done at Ottawa today, but they are done in accordance with recognized procedure, and to leave this with the general officer commanding the command might lead to a lack of uniformity in practice, which could be achieved only through the direction of army headquarters itself.
So that in the end, in order to secure uniformity of practice and coordination, it would be necessary that ultimately it should come to army headquarters and should form the subject matter of a regulation, and that in the endi it should be done under the responsibility of the minister. I am afraid you cannot escape from that as long as you have our system of responsible and representative institutions, and it seems to me that putting it in this form does recognize the importance of cadet corps. It recognizes and gives effect to the desirability of having coordination at headquarters, and also-and this is one of the most important features-it permits of changes and developments as they may occur. We have had in effect commands as the major military organizations in Canada-I refer to the organization of Canada into five commands-for a matter of only some months now, and it may be necessary at some future time to change that organization. We have changed it from districts and we are changing it now into commands, provided that this bill is carried; and it may be desirable for cadet corps purposes to have some other organization.
It may be desirable that the officer commanding areas as well as the officer commanding commands should have power to deal with cadets. In order to have some element of
Militia Act

flexibility, it is necessary that the power to do it should) not be set forth expressly in the statute and given to some designated' officer but should foe reserved for exercise by the minister.
With regard to section 61, under the law as it stands today cadets corps shall be drilled and trained as prescribed, and* may be furnished with arms, ammunition and equipment under conditions prescribed-prescribed by whom? By the governor in council. That is as it stands today, and) if that is a desirable way of conducting cadet corps work in Canada, then I think the world has turned upside down. We must get away from referring everything to the governor in council, and the one person who has to take responsibility under our system is the minister. I submit you might as well put that in the statute and have done with it there.
With regard to some of the other points, the hon. member for Peterborough West asked if the minister had authority to discontinue a cadet corps. Under the existing provisions, in section 59, the minister had and has the authority to authorize the formation of cadet corps, and I am advised that that includes authority to disband them. The answer therefore is yes. He asked if there would be a reduction in the number of cadet corps. There will be no reduction in the number of cadet corps of boys who fall within the classes I mentioned, aged fourteen to eighteen, provided that they are organized in corps of twenty or more.
As regards the question asked by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche, I shall have the answer at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
