speechtext:
I am very much obliged to the hon. member for his remarks. I must say that if I had been in this job longer I might have made the statement earlier. But I would draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the representatives of the cadet corps, the navy league and the air cadets have been communicated with and are familiar with the situation. I believe it would be the unanimous wish of the house that I should convey our thanks to the organizations which have carried on this valuable work before, during and since the war. I refer to schools which have operated school cadet corps and those who have interested themselves in the operation of open cadet corps in the army, as well also to all those who have worked with them, including particularly the masters, teachers and instructors who have devoted a good part of their time to this work, and also those other friends of the schools, of the bo.vs and of this movement who have contributed generously to its support. I should like to refer also to the very special position of the navy league in connection with sea cadets. They started this work long before the first war and, as I have said, they were supported by the army with grants of money in respect of each cadet, as weli as other assistance, including support with respect to camps. I regret that, owing to circumstances over which I had no control, it was not possible to discuss with the representatives of the navy league the arrangements which I believe will ultimately be found by them to be thoroughly satisfactory. Things had to be done in order to acquaint various units and formations with what was happening; and owing to the circumstances I have indicated it was found impossible to discuss with them, as I should have liked, the details of this plan. I can tell hon. members, however, that just today I received a communication from them asking for an interview, and I shall be glad to see their representatives as soon as possible in order to arrive at a workable arrangement.
With regard to the air cadet league, we were able to see their representatives and work out with them the main details of the plan which I have announced. I am going to meet them again next week and discuss further with them the details on which we can cooperate for the good of their movement and the good of Canada.
I should add that in all the work of this department so far we have tried to cooperate with the people interested in the various fields. For example. I have already had a meeting

Militia Act
with the council of reserve associations with regard to the reserves of the army, and with a number of other agencies. In every possible way we aim to cooperate with them in seeing what can be done to meet the particular problem. I hold out to hon. members here, as to those agencies in support of which they have spoken, the warmest offer of complete cooperation in these fields in which we are all interested.
Might I now answer the questions asked by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche. I find that before I entered the department a communication was received from the province of Quebec Catholic school trustees' association forwarding a resolution adopted November 13, 1946, in which they protested against the continuation of cadets of all classes in their schools. I have only this to say, that the arrangement under which cadets have been established in the schools goes back to an agreement with most of the provinces which was arrived at under the Strathcona trust. The date of the agreement with Quebec was 1911. Under that agreement the training carried out is provided for, and cadet corps are organized only by written request of the sponsor; that is, the educational association. I might quote from the regulations for the cadet services of Canada. Paragraph 8 reads:
8.	If the proposed cadet corps is connected with an educational institution, MFB 252 will be signed by the headmaster or principal of the school, and "the secretary or other officials of the school board; and if under the jurisdiction of provincial educational authorities will also bear the written sanction of the minister, superintendent or other official head of the department of education of the province, or of the chairman of the school board concerned.
Paragraph 9 continues:
9.	Cadet corps of the Royal Canadian Army Cadets shall be divided into
(a) school cadet corps formed under the sponsorship of the proper school authorities.
So I would say to my hon. friend that anything done so far has been done with the cooperation and sponsorship of the school authorities, and with regard to our work in this field we hope we may continue to have that cooperation and sponsorship.
With regard to the other question, as to the methods used for the recruiting of the cadet corps, I can only say that this is not a matter which falls within the scope of the work of this department. It is done by the cadet corps themselves. In some cadet corps and some schools it is completely voluntary. In some schools there is a certain element which may regard it as the thing to do in the school, and there may be other situations. But as far as our department is concerned we have nothing whatever to do with the recruitment. When
the cadets are recruited we pay the per capita amount of $1 for senior cadets and, up to now, fifty cents for junior cadets. We pay $2 for each member of the band, and give assistance in the way of contributions toward1 the expenses of uniforms, camps and so on. So far it has worked out well, and I hope it will work out well in the future.

Realizing that the hon.
member for Nanaimo has withdrawn his amendment, I would say to the minister just two things. One is that I feel keenly that there is a latent danger in section 19, for the reasons I endeavoured to point out this afternoon, reasons which the minister well knows are not directed against him or his present office.
Second, I hope the minister will give further consideration to the possibility of having cadet corps in at least some of the primary schools. It may be that there are local deterrent factors in some areas across Canada which would make enrolment of young boys in cadet corps undesirable. On the other hand, likewise and conversely there are schools where such enrolment is desirable. Before any sweeping decision is made, I suggest to the minister that an analysis be made of some centres where this might be possible, rather than having one sweeping order.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Under section 60 of the
old Militia Act the commanding officer of a district was in charge of cadet instruction. He delegated his responsibilities to boards of education across the country. The general officer commanding No. 2 military district, which takes in Hamilton, Niagara and Toronto areas, and from which a large number of
Militia Act

cadets come, would appoint officers within the jurisdiction of the various school boards, and those boards would have absolute control over the school cadet system.
At this stage I object to the minister's changing all that, and substituting for it central authority here in Ottawa under some officers nominated by the minister. It can be made a huge machine of political propaganda. I must voice my objections strongly, coming as I do from Ontario, a province from which the greater portion of the cadets have been drawn for years. That is the old province which did so well in all the wars, from the Fenian raids to the northwest rebellion and the South African war, followed by the two great wars of our generation. The cadet system in our country was good enough for those times.
I do not think it is fair for the minister to take this stand, although he is a good man and was a good soldier. Unfortunately we have no minister from the Toronto district, nor have we had one since 1935. Surely this is highly dangerous to provincial rights and property and civil rights in the provinces. Here we find the head of a department, who comes from a sister province, upsetting everything that has been done in our province. I say, "hands off the schools in our province." Our educational system is adequate for our province, and it has always had a cadet system which was one of the best in the whole country, and did its duty in two long wars.
I was member of a school board for some time, and I have discussed this matter with school principals. I say it is not proper to have one cadet system in the schools, and another system outside the schools, cadets spending time from their studies at night, and to have drilling two nights a week by some officer appointed by the minister. I can tell you this, that you are upsetting the whole system. If I were the only member in the House of Commons from my province, I would still say that in that province we have had a cadet system which has produced results.
A survey of the public and separate schools, and also the secondary schools in Ontario would show that in two wars there have been large numbers of enlistments from those schools. I have before me a report showing that at one of the annual commencements of one of the secondary schools in my district there were about 2,000 enlistments in the last war. Nearly 500 from those schools were killed in the war just passed. But to change the whole cadet system, and have it done 
down here at Ottawa, is all wrong, and I protest against it. I do so in the name of the people whom I have the honour to represent.
I have discussed this matter with school principals on several occasions. We have two representatives from the separate schools on the board of education in our city, who had no information whatever about the change, and this subject of cadet training was discussed last Thursday evening by the board. It is known that cadet officers give their time free of charge after school hours. Some of them give physical drill, while others coach football, hockey and other sports, and cadet work after school.
Cadets from Oakwood collegiate, Riverdale collegiate and Malvern collegiate have won rifle-shooting matches conducted by the militia. Any change in the present system would be grossly unfair to the school boards, municipalities in Ontario. The minister, who represents the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George should not come into Ontario and say that he is going to upset the whole thing and run the national cadet system from Ottawa. I do not say he would do so intentionally, or anything like that. But it is stated clearly in the bill1 that the minister has authority to nominate someone in Ottawa to take charge of the cadets for him.
I realize that some of my hon. friends to my left do not believe in cadets any more than they believe in war. They believe in peace pacts, and all that sort of thing. But they have been proven to be wrong. Since confed1-eration the backbone of the Militia Act has been the boards of education and the cadet corps of public schools, high schools and vocational schools. It was a cheap way', without much expense to the government to have this done, because the local boards provided uniforms and other essentials. They used to have wooden rifles for drill purposes in the public schools, and the chief drill officers contributed a great- deal to the welfare of the corps.
I wish to protest against this gross invasion of provincial rights. Here we have two systems, one of which has been in the schools since 1877, and the other of which is to be outside, taking up the time of cadets from their studies at night. I tell- you this, that what the government suggests here is a waste of public money.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
There is one point I should like to emphasize. I have heard several views expressed this afternoon and this evening. My personal experience is that fourteen y'ears of age is young enough for a lad to be enrolled in a regular cadet corps. If a lad

Militia Act
is taken under fourteen years, and goes to camp for a period in the summer for purposes of training, he is of no use at all. He is homesick, he is too young, and he has to be watched everj' minute. It has been generally found that fourteen years is young enough, and I approve the age limit of fourteen to eighteen years. I think the minister knows that, as far as the navy league and the sea cadet movements are concerned, that was felt to be the case months ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: All this talk about cadet training seems to be too much one-sided. There seems to be everything for the boys and nothing for the girls. It is well known that the girls in the nursing profession and in other occupations covered themselves with glory during the last war. Girls are just as' proud of their physical fitness as the boys and they rise to as great heights as is shown by the fine young girl from the city of Ottawa.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Every hon. member who has spoken during the last ten minutes has said that there is just one point to be cleared up, and the same holds true with me. I am concerned with the concentrated authority which is vested in the minister by the new sections 60 and 61. Under the new section 60, he will have the authority to appoint the officer to command, and under the new section 61, he has the authority to control and train cadets. That is pretty plenary authority to place in the minister, and as far as I am concerned it is too plenary an authority.
The cadet system is the real bulwark of our militia, but we do not train cadets simply to be soldiers of the future. We try to train them in the arts of citizenship. We all know that young men properly trained in the cadet system become fine citizens. It was my privilege to be at Niagara camp in July, 1914, just before world war I. There were with me quite a number of cadets from the part of the country from which I come, and after that time most of those young men joined up in the armed forces. As a matter of fact you could not find more than six young men in the district of Parkdale who were not in the armed forces in one way or another. Their training as cadets had built up character, leadership, the ability to take orders, respect for constituted authority and respect for Canadian citizenship.
There have been in this house hon. members who attained positions of prominence but who did not have the same regard for the cadet training system that we who sit on this side have. The minister straightened out a lot of thoughts in the minds of hon. members on this
side with his statement late this afternoon. However, the day may come when we may have somebody sitting in his place who has not the same regard for the cadet system as we on this side have and as apparently he has. Things may be done in a slothful manner and we cannot tolerate that type of leadership in the cadet system. Without proper leadership we are going to have inefficiency and the cadet system is likely to fall into disgrace or contempt among the youth of the country. If that should happen we shall have dealt a sorry blow to the citizenry of this country and to our future progress.
Had the hon. members for Nanaimo not withdrawn his amendment, I was going to move an amendment to the new sections 60 and 61 and ask that the word "minister" be struck out in both sections and that the words "governor in council" be substituted therefor. I feel that this is something that strikes at the very heart of the future of this country and of the young men whom we are setting up to lead. I am not going to move that amendment, but I suggest to the minister that he consider whether too much authority is not being concentrated in himself under these sections and whether it should not fall upon the governor in council.
I think that way of handling the matter would be the best way of dealing with the problems that come up in connection with cadet training. I should like him to explain his remark that the system would be turned upside down if the work of the department were carried on by the governor in council instead of by himself as minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

They are not in charge of the cadets since previously cadets came under the ordinary command of the district officers commanding and now they will come under the command of the general officers commanding; that is, if this bill passes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
This section gives the governor in council the power to say when the Canadian army may be called out for any military purpose other than drill or training. There are certain sections of the criminal code which would have to be read into this. Under the old Militia Act and the criminal code, a mayor, warden or sheriff could ask the commanding officer of the district for military aid to support the civil police in case of strike or riot. When some of the troops came home after the last war they complained because all the licences had been given to foreign born people who had never served a day in the forces and there was a serious state of affairs for three or four days, and a riot accordingly. It was not necessary to ask for the aid of the militia, but the mayor and the warden and the sheriff had the power to summon them.
In the case of the strike at Hamilton, a number of troops were called into the district. Power is now being given under section 20 to the minister and to the governor in council alone to do this. The governor in council may be on holidays, as he frequently is, for three or four months in the year and, if application for aid were made, aid would not be available. They called out the soldiers to clean snow along the tracks of the railroads during the bad storm in the first year of the war. They were used for many other purposes for which they should not have been used, and got $1.30 a day, and for snow cleaning they got $4.85 or $3.85 or whatever it was and Ottawa refused to let soldiers get the extra pay. Was that the right way to use a civilian army? Are these men no longer citizens of Canada when they don the king's uniform? What right have we to take away from soldiers their rights and privileges as citizens? Ottawa never knows what the rest of the country is thinking. You have to go back to the constituencies to find out what the people are really thinking. This section gives altogether too much power to the governor in council, and it is not in the interests of the Canadian army and the defence of this country.
Britain made leases of Atlantic bases, with the United States leasing for ninety-nine years naval bases all the way from Newfoundland to British Guiana. Those leases should now be cancelled and charged up to lease-lend. The action was taken to protect American shores in the Battle of the Atlantic, but the leases should now be cancelled.

Two of the greatest wars were fought without the governor in council being given such tremendous powers as are sought by this bill. They would enable the governor in council to make a political football of militia and defence in this country.

The Army Act for the time being in force in Great Britain, the king's regulations, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this act or the regulations made hereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia . . .

It seems to me that we in Canada should have an army act of our own to govern our own army. But this amendment does not do that. That seems to me a poor way to build up an army act of our own. This parliament should have its own army act to govern our Canadian army. dian army in matters of discipline. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I rise for the purpose of asking the minister why it is that he is asking for so many powers to make regulations. So far as this rewriting of the Militia Act is concerned, it seems to consist in placing under the governor in council the widest possible powers to make regulations, and it is certainly indicative of the power complex of this government. As I look over this bill I find that practically every section gives the governor in council power to make regulations, and if I read the bill correctly most of these regulations do not even have to be laid on the table of parliament. There is a provision a little later on with regard to
laying regulations on the table of parliament, but here again the minister is made allpowerful because, under the proposed new section 140, the governor in council can simply certify that publication might endanger the safety of the state or convey secret or confidential information to a foreign power, in which case the governor in council can make applicable to the army laws which in no way would be known to anyone but the governor in council. This bill goes much farther than any other bill which has been brought before the house. A mass of comprehensive powers has been granted to the governor in council to make regulations.
Some years ago this matter came up before the British parliament, and I hold in my hand a summary of the recommendations which were made under which the king in council might pass regulations which would become the law of the land without anybody knowing anything about them. The committee report to which I refer is that of the. Lord Sankey committee which convened in 1929. It was pointed out that certain powers must be vested in the king in council; but with a view to exercising some control over the absolutism of the king in council the committee recommended that, whenever a regulation or order was passed, certain things should be done. First, it should be laid on the table of parliament; second, with a view to controlling the multiplicity of regulations which are being passed by governments today, not only should all the regulations passed be laid on the table of parliament, but there should be a permanent committee of the house set up to examine them. That recommendation of the Sankey committee has been more or less accepted by the British House of Commons.
I suggested that the time has come to call a halt to the relentless march of this government toward government of the country by the governor in council or by the minister. We cannot stop it because we have not the power in parliament to do so, even though parliament is starting to regain some of its powers since hon. members are beginning to exercise their independence, something that was foreign to parliament within the period of war. I suggest that something should be done toward setting up a nermanent standing committee of parliament, to which all regulations and all orders in council should be submitted. That committee would have no power to change the substantive regulations which are made; but it would have the power to place 'before members of parliament, who do not have the opportunity of studying these
Militia Act

orders in council and regulations, something of what has been done under order in council or by regulation.
As I understand the situation in Britain, what they do is this: the House of Commons submits these regulations to a committee. The committee reports on the regulations placed before it; first, as to whether any matter of principle is involved; second, whether any regulations or rule imposes a tax; third, whether a regulation or rule is challenged either permanently or never challengeable; fourth, whether is consists wholly or partly of consolidation; fifth, whether there is any special feature of the regulation or rule meriting the attention of the house; sixth, whether there were any circumstances connected with the work of the regulation or rule meriting such attention; seventh, whether the regulation or rule should be starred. By starring, I simply mean whether it should be brought to the attention of the house and the country so that the house and the countiy will appreciate what is being done.
During the last few days I have had occasion to run through the series of orders in council which will be attached to the omnibus bill. These orders in council and regulations were in effect during the period of the war. I have endeavoured to follow somewhat carefully the orders in council so passed. Many of these orders in council I had no idea of at all. Many of them took away the right of recourse to the courts; others denied the liberty of the individual. Still others gave to the minister the power of arbitrary decision in favour of one person, while denying another person the benefit of the principle of equality under the law. Today we are passing a bill which allows the governor in council absolute powers, concentrates in his person power in reference to the armed forces of this country the like of which no minister has ever before exercised. If we pass it and give the power we shall have no realization whatever of the power we are granting.
Is the minister in a position to tell the committee just why it is so necessary for the governor in council and himself to have the powers for which he is asking at this time? In reply to the hon. member for Melfort a moment ago, the minister said that, so far as section 69 was concerned, it was necessary to pass it in the form in which it was before it has been passed upon by the house because it would take time to sort out the king's regulations and orders or those applicable to the army in the United Kingdom. Well, we have got along for a long time under these regulations, and if the government is to introduce a measure to change these things,
[Mr. Diefenbaker.3
why does it do so in this haphazard manner? For the life of me, I cannot understand it. The other day I asked the minister how many regulations had been passed and he said that thousands of them had been passed. Then I asked him for particulars because under the act it is necessary to place them before parliament or at least to have them printed in the Canada Gazette. When I asked him whether or not these regulations appeared in the Canada Gazette his answer was, "Of course, not the thousands but some of them."

I would call the attention of the committee to the clause we are discussing, namely, section 24. That is the one we have reached and it would ask that there be substituted for section 93 of the Militia Act, as it has stood since 1868, a provision reading:
The governor in council may make regulations for the convening of courts of inquiry and the composition thereof for the purpose of investigating and reporting on any matter connected with the government or discipline of the Canadian army or with the conduct of any officer or man thereof.
And then subsection 2:
The governor in council may make regulations for the convening of courts-martial and the jurisdiction and composition thereof for the purpose of trying any officer or man of the Canadian army for any offence under this act or for the purpose of trying any other persons punishable under this act.
Let us contrast what we want to introduce with what there was before and see on what thin and narrow grounds this harangue of the hon. member opposite has been based. Section 93, as it stood, reads:
The governor in council may convene courts of inquiry and appoint officers of the militia to constitute such courts, for the purpose of investigating and reporting on any matter connected with the government or discipline of the militia, or with the conduct of any officer or man of the force; and may, at any time, convene courts-martial and delegate power to convene 83166-33
such courts, and to appoint officers to constitute them, for the purpose of trying any officer or man of the militia for any offence under this act, and may also delegate power to approve, confirm, mitigate or remit any sentence of any such court.
Neither in that clause nor in any other clause in this bill do you find any increase in the power of the governor in council. There is no increase whatever. If there is, I should like to hear about it and I would consider it. But I have gone over it and have not found one instance.

The purpose of the
amendment is to enable the governor in council to make regulations so that the governor in council shall not have to do this job every time and so give my hon. friend an opportunity for making his attacks upon it for passing too many orders in council. These attacks really have gone on too long.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I venture to say that in no country on earth has less power been given to ministers and to the officers concerned with the administration of military affairs than in Canada. Power has almost all reposed either in parliament or in the governor in council, and for that reason the governor in council has been forced to pass this great number, indeed thousands, of orders of which my hon. friend subsequently complains. If he were in England or in the United States he would not find any such number of orders in council. Why? Because it is done by others inferior to the body corresponding to the governor in council. That is so in every case. It is extraordinary that this stuff should go on, because we have here in Canada, due to the fact that so many matters are required to be done by governor in council, the complaint that it is undemocratic. ' But in England, in the United States, in Australia and New Zealand, in all the democracies, my hon. friend will not find that the powers here exercised by the governor in council with regard to military matters are exorcised by parliament. He will find that they are exercised by some military officer or by a minister, in every single case of which I know anything.
This complaint about government by order in council should be made on the other score; that is, on the score that the governor in council is now required under our law to do too much and that responsibility is therefore removed from the persons who should be responsible in these and other cases; in many

Militia Act

instances the minister and in other instances the officers of the armed forces or of the responsible department concerned.
My hon. friend referred to the discussion we had last week about regulations, when he asked how many regulations had been adopted under the Militia Act in 1946, and some other hon. member inquired about 1938. I did not know the number and I do not think it was surprising that I did not.

No, but I now have the regulations here. They are in these bound volumes which were duly laid on the table of the house. They have been published in the Canada Gazette and the law has been completely complied with regarding them.
With regard to 1938, to answer that question, since this is the first opportunity I have had, there were 333 orders and regulations made pursuant to the powers vested in the governor in council or the Minister of National Defence by the Militia Act. Of these, two-thirds were made by the governor in council and one-third by the minister. Twenty-six of the orders to amend king's regulations, Canada, were made by the governor in council. During 1946 there 'were 985 orders and regulations made pursuant to the powers vested in the governor in council or the Minister of National Defence by the Militia Act. Of these, about half were made by the governor in council and about half by the minister pursuant to the powers vested in him by the act and by order in council P.C. 44/3723, dated May 4, 1942. By this order the governor in council, under powers conferred, delegated to the minister powei to amend establishments within ten per cent limits. Had it not been for this order, most of the orders made by the minister during 1946 would have had to be made by the governor in council. Of the orders made by the governor in council in 1946, 28 amended K.R. (Can.). In addition to those which deal with establishments, the strength of forces, the provision of supplies and so on, many huu dreds of orders were made by the governo* m council during 1946 on the submission of the Minister of National Defence, dealing with the following matters: the grant of pensions and gratuities to retiring members of the permanent force, pursuant to the provisions of the Militia Pension Act. I ask the hon. member: does he think that should be done by parliament?

Then, second: the approval of leases, contracts and other agreements entered into by the department; third, the approval of settlement of all claims in excess of $200 made against the department. During the war years there were hundreds of orders of this kind, which I submit should never have had to be dealt with by the governor in council. In 1946 there were 985. If my hon. friend looks through these orders relative to the armed forces of Canada he will see that first they come out as general orders, published in the Canada Gazette, and then are laid on the table of the house. Let me read the list of the orders in one issue, Tanuary 28, 1944: "Financial regulations and instructions for the Canadian active service force; amendments. Financial regulations and instructions for the Canadian active service force; amendments. Officers, maximum ages for holding appointments and for retirements. Conversion and redesignation, active units," and so on. They deal with matters affecting the administration of the armed forces, matters which certainly should be dealt with, not by parliament, but by the governor in council; or, in cases where no question of policy is involved, where it is merely the application of a routine order or dealing with a situation that has to be dealt with without any question of principle involved, then it should be dealt with by the minister or by someone delegated by the minister.
That is the way it is done in England; that is the way it is done in the United States. The reason my hon. friend has been able to make so much of this plea of -his that there -has been government by order in council in Canada is that the governor in council has done things which in other countries would be done by subordinate officials or bodies. That accounts for a very large proportion of the orders to which he has referred. Take these other things; take the approval of an appointment, promotion or retirement. Under our practice that is recommended to the governor in council by the minister. It be-

Militia Act
comes part of a long order. It is printed in the Canada Gazette. It is laid on the table of the house. These are all good and adequate safeguards; but to suggest that it should be done by any other process involving an application to parliament is to ignore totally the proper functions of parliament, of the executive and of the administration.
I am sorry to have delayed the committee on this matter, Mr. Chairman, but here it is a question whether the governor in council shall convene courts of inquiry or make regulations under which courts of inquiry shall be convened. That is the point. I submit that in this year 1947 the governor in council should be too busy to convene courts of inquiry and that this should be done as it has been done, in fact; that is. by the convening of courts of inquiry under regulations. That is all this and the other changes mean, that we are trying to get a machinery which is workable and sensible and responsible, where the whole operation is not related to the horse and buggy days when we had a totally different set-up in Canada, a machinery under which we shall be able to carry on government as efficiently and as responsibly as possible.

speechtext: The explanation by the minister is the position commonly taken by those who have not an answer. I asked the minister why he found it so necessary to ask at this time for the power to make regulations when, over the years, that power had not rested in the minister or the governor in council?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Then why the
amendment? That was my question a while ago. Of course the minister found it necessary to deal with everything but what I dealt with. I asked him the question, recognizing the need for regulations on occasion, whether or not consideration would be given by the government to following the British system, whereby regulations and orders in council are available to a committee of the House of Commons for investigating, consideration and recommendation. To that suggestion the minister made no reference at all. When he talks about this not being an order in council government and becomes very much annoyed when I suggest that it is, let us look at the record for a moment. The question I asked the other day was, how many regulations or orders in council were passed in 1946? The answer by the responsible minister was, "Several thousand". I asked him whether he said "Seven thousand" and he said, "Several thousand". Now he says the total is 985.
83166-33i
The minister says that this is not an order in council government. Well, let us look at the record. Between 1914 and 1917, three years of war, the total number of orders in council passed in this country, according to an answer given in the house at that time, was some 790 odd, and I speak from memory. During a similar period of this war, when parliament was circumvented on every possible occasion by the government, over 85,000 orders in council were passed. The number for the period of the war was approximately 90,000, and this government has not yet learned that the war is over, because orders in council are still pouring out in numbers far and beyond anything they could possibly defend. And here we are in 1947 with a bill before parliament for the purpose of ratifying and making part of the law of the land a whole raft of orders in council which have never been read by most members of parliament, if by any; which deny the right of recourse to the courts, which permit of discrimination as between individual and individual, which allow the minister power to say to one person, "This is your right", and to the other person, "You have no such right", and denies the person discriminated against the right of recourse to the courts.
The minister in this instance asks for power to make himself the absolute ruler of the armed forces of this country. This afternoon the hon. member for Greenwood made a most reasoned appeal, and pointed out that the minister will make himself all-powerful and absolute-. Every one of the sections passed here this evening, and those which will follow, seem designed to do one thing, namely, to place in the hand of this minister power which no other minister in a government has ever asked to have placed in him. He has absolute power to do the different things set out in the sections which have already been passed, and to which I shall not refer.
But when one suggests that some curb be put on this absolute power, on this power complex, the answer one receives is that it is not a serious matter. I think he called it "stuff". "Stuff"?-yes; this attitude on the part of the government, in circumventing parliament and short-circuiting parliament by allowing the council chamber to be the -place where laws are made, is the stuff of which autocracy is made.
That is the reason I rise at this time. I started out to ask my hon, friend a- simple question. Would he, as a democrat, be prepared to consider the setting up of a standing committee of parliament, so that many of these things which must necessarily be passed by regulation could be made known to the country, and members of the House of Com-
Militia Act

mons could be made aware of their contents, to the end that unfairness shall not be permitted to creep into the law of this country by the back-door method of orders in council? I still ask him that. He defends what is done; he cannot do anything else. This government stands indicted as a government which has ruled by decree, and is still trying to rule by decree.
With parliament today to some extent regaining its lost prerogatives, prerogatives which it lost during the period of the war- and it started back in 1914, so that parliament has gradually been receding-will the minister not at least give some consideration to placing this parliament in the same position that is enjoyed today by the British parliament, namely, that of giving it the opportunity to consider through a committee these orders, so as to prevent discrimination, to assure that justice shall be done and equality under the law maintained?
That was the only reason for my question originally, and I do not see why there should have been such heat. But, sir, the reason for the heat is that, though in the past my hon. friend has talked against orders in council, he realizes that today the government with which he is associated has now denied to parliament in too many instances its sovereign right either to pass legislation or, if it delegates the power to pass legislation, then to have the right to review it.
I ask the minister once more if he will give consideration to putting into effect what has been found necessary in Great Britain, namely, a standing committee, to the end that these matters may be examined so as to ensure fairness and equality.

speechtext:
I must reply again to the hon. member, although I thought I had answered him fully. These general orders for the years 1944, 1945 and 1946 were laid before him and other hon. members, placed on the table of the house, in accordance with the law, at the first session of parliament after they were passed. Furthermore, they were published in the Canada Gazette as they came out. They were passed in accordance with the law. I do not see what cause for complaint he has, when he did nothing about the matter except make the kind of speech he makes tonight.
So far as I know, there has been no motion -and any hon. member may make such a motion-to have an order brought before the house. But there has been nothing of that kind. I have not heard from my predecessors any complaint as to what has been done. Whatever was done was done in accordance

with the law as laid down by parliament; and it has been done in that way because there was no simpler way to do it.
Let me just ask the hon. member who he thinks should pass the laws regarding the matters I shall set out. Who does he think, and who do hon. members in the committee think should deal with these questions: (1) adding one pistol or one rifle or one round of pistol or rifle ammunition to the establishment of an infantry battalion to meet operational needs; or (2) adding one cook to the establishment of a training centre to take ca,re of varying recruit intake; or (3) changing the name or establishment title of a "headquarters transport company" to a "corps headquarters transport company"; or (4) changing the title of an artillery regiment from towed guns to self-propelled guns; or (5) providing an additional pigeon loft as a unit of the army for operational use in a theatre of war?
Under the existing law, dating from 1868, all these matters have to be done by orders in council; and that is why we have so many order's in council.

speechtext: Hon. BROOKE CLANTON (Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the Department of National Defence Act.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
When this bill was in the resolution stage we expressed general approval of the underlying principle, namely, that of consolidating the three fighting services under one minister. That is a policy which we have frequently advocated and we are heartily in agreement with it. Following further, we find that there is to be one deputy minister and there are to be three associate deputy ministers. I consider that we must ask the minister to give us a little more information regarding the duties of these three associate deputy ministers. One cannot help feeling, from the little information that we have at the present time, that a department which is headed by a minister and a deputy minister is rather top-heavy if it has three associate deputy ministers as well.
We were told during the resolution stage that one of these associate deputy ministers would look after finance and supply, that the second would look after personnel, but we did not have any information as to what the third associate deputy minister would do. I rather gathered that he would be an associate deputy minister at large, taking on such duties as might be assigned to him from time to time. I am heartily in accord with any steps that can be taken to unite the three services, letting them function with a common doctrine and working toward a common end, but we must

National Defence Act
safeguard the functions of the officers of the various forces and we must see to it that there is no overlapping or duplication.
I cannot help thinking that if you have certain senior officers in the three services charged with the responsibility of looking after personnel it should hardly be necessary to appoint an associate deputy minister to coordinate the work of those three senior officers. I hope therefore the minister will take the time to explain in greater detail the functions of these officials he is now appointing.
We agree with the formation of a research board, and the minister gave us information regarding the functions of that body. I wrant to throw out one possible suggestion having to do with the important matter of civil defence in war of today. During the last war, civil defence in Canada was under the department of the Secretary of State. I think I am correct in that statement. I suggest to the minister that civil defence is an integral part of the defence of the country, and in the event of hostilities breaking out at some future day civil1 defence might well receive the consideration of the Department of National Defence. I consider it wrong that it should be entirely separated from national defence and put under a separate department. I merely offer that as a suggestion for the minister's further consideration. I do not intend to debate it any further today, but I think it is something that might well be examined to see whether civil defence should not be brought under the Department of National Defence instead of being left to an entirely different department. I would therefore ask the minister now to explain in rather greater detail than he has so far given the functions of these deputy ministers and to assure us that there will be no duplication of effort and no overlapping of the legitimate duties of the officers of these departments.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon. gentleman's remarks. The effort, as he says, is to consolidate the three departments of defence, as they were and as they grew up during the war, into one department, and for that purpose it has been put forward in this bill that there should be a single deputy minister of defence and not more than three associate deputy ministers. As I told the house when the matter was under consideration last week, there are at present two associate deputy ministers. One has charge of finance, supply, equipment, and similar matters, and the other has charge of personnel and pay.
At the present time there is no intention of appointing a third, but in the course of S3166-34
developing the work of the department we may find that there is a natural division to which effect should be given and that we should have one associate deputy minister in charge of finance and administration, a second in charge of supply, equipment, engineering and so on, corresponding to the Q and M.G.O. branches of the army, and a third in charge of personnel and pay, corresponding to the A branch of the army. At the present time, however, we believe we have divided the work in a sensible way so that we can get along with two associate deputies. They are carrying on well, and we believe they will be able to carry on.
The hon. member asked whether there would be any duplication of work with the armed services. The committee appreciates that the armed services themselves have branches corresponding to administration, supply and personnel; but in the matters involving financial responsibility their submissions go through the civilian side of the department. Further, I should point out that in addition to the men in the armed forces, there is a considerable group of civilians who are working for the department. For example, there are not only the civil servants on the headquarters staff at Ottawa and elsewhere throughout Canada; large groups of prevailing rate employees are working at the various depots, dockyards and so on. That number totals something of the magnitude of twenty thousand at the present time, so that there is a full-time job for an associate deputy minister in charge of personnel and pay on the civilian side because of his purely civilian duties in addition to those he will have as the channel by means of which submissions from the armed forces with regard to many matters will reach the minister.
With regard to the final question on civil defence, I may tell the hon. member we have that in mind. During the war, civil defence was under the Department of National War Services, working in conjunction with other departments. Our thought is that in peace time we in the Department of National Defence should do planning, in conjunction with other departments, for example, health and welfare, and that we should be prepared, should any emergency arise, to deal with that very important question. The hon. member probably would also include in his definition of civil defence the combined subjects of research and industrial organization, and both those are being looked after as well. Only recently the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps Association was formed, as an association of men in the services and those in industry, who worked together so effectively in war to

National Defence Act

produce the great quantities of material that helped all the allied countries to achieve final victory. They have formed an association so that it might be a continuing and developing branch of our total preparation for any emergency that might arise. The president of the association is Mr. Victor Sifton of Winnipeg, who during the war was a distinguished master-general of the ordnance, though in a civilian capacity. He came there after having had a fine record in the first war, and he is taking on this work in connection with the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps Association which we regard as of the utmost importance.

Subsection 3 provides:
Each associate deputy minister of national defence shall have the rank and status of a deputy head of a department . . .
In reading that, I recall that last session the veterans affairs committee had to deal with a similar clause. At that time there were two deputy ministers of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and one gentleman who had the administration of an important section of the department prior to last session was given the rank and status of a deputy minister. The committee discussed that matter at considerable length, and I think I am correct in saying that finally the committee agreed unanimously that in our opinion there should be only one deputy head of the department. In this case we actually have suggested three associate deputy ministers, each to be given the rank and status of deputy head of a department.
I should like to ask the minister two questions. In view of the action of the veterans affairs committee last session in dealing with the Department of Veterans Affairs, does the minister not think this is a somewhat unfair and unnecessary situation? Then could he explain to the committee the policy of the government in granting the associate deputy ministers the rank and status of a deputy minister? I am afraid this section might be the cause of some friction and possibly some difficulty as between departments of this government.

It was felt that, because we had had three departments and three people who at one time or another held the position of deputy

minister of one or other of those departments, we should continue, because of their distinguished record of service and their important positions in the new department, to give them the rank and status of a deputy minister.

speechtext: The minister said something about planning for the production of weapons. He did not go into any great detail on that subject. We all know it is of the utmost importance that the country should be able to produce these weapons of war. What is the present arrangement? subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD

With regard to procurement, however, it would have come under the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. In view of the fact that the supply side of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply is not likely to continue very much longer, we have under the most active consideration the development of a machinery of government under which there would be, first, planning; second, the development of specifications; third, the encouragement of development work; fourth, the development of people with required skills; and fifth, research in design. All these, of course, envisage a close cooperation between research and national defence and the procurement agency of the government selected to do the job. I must say it is not intended at the present time that procurement will be a function of the Department of National Defence. We envisage that being carried on permanently by some other agency of government, and the exact machinery is now being worked out.

Then, if this bill passes, research will come under the defence research board, which will report through the Minister of National Defence.
