speechtext: I take it that the government's policy is to depend upon private firms being prepared to manufacture weapons, and that there is to be some sort of cooperation with private firms. The minister mentioned procurement. I understand that at present that comes under the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. But the other day the Prime Minister said that all the buying for the forces was to be done by a crown company known as Canadian Commercial Corporation, under the Department of Trade and Commerce. If all the buying is to be done by the Department of Trade and Commerce, does that not push the Department of Reconstruction and Supply out of the job of acting as procurement agency; and does it not also weaken your plan for being in a position to have weapons made effectively? After all, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply is interested in manufacturing, while the Department of Trade and Commerce is a buying and selling department. How does the minister purpose getting around that difficulty?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
The hon. member has referred to a matter I had touched upon, and that is that we were aiming to have procurement dealt with by the Department of Trade and Commerce, using the agency of a crown corporation, in that it will take over the functions of the Department of Munitions and Supply, as exercised during the war, and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply since the war. It will take over also many of the top personnel, so that there will be complete continuity. It is our hope that there will be no interruption whatsoever.
May I tell the hon. member that, so far as procurement is concerned, we are fairly well equipped with most weapons at the present time. We are not in the market for any large quantities of them. We are more concerned with keeping our ideas and our planning up to date, through intelligence work, cooperation with other governments, research 83166-34J
in our own country, and through cooperation with industry in our own country. We are now developing those lines of cooperation.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
But is not cooperation with industry the key factor in being in a position to have weapons made quickly and properly? The Department of Reconstruction and Supply has been in a first-class position to cooperate with industry. However, now that the minister is giving the work of procurement to the Department of Trade and Commerce, is he not losing a great deal of efficiency in connection with cooperation with industry? The Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned primarily with buying and selling. In fact the crown company to which the minister has referred is concerned with buying and selling abroad.
Would it not be far better for the Department of National Defence to set up some machinery of its own for cooperation with industry, rather than having to deal through another department, such as the Department of Trade and Commerce? I suggest to the minister we are far more likely to be in a position to get up-to-date weapons if the cooperation with industry is through the Department of National Defence, rather than through the Department of Trade and Commerce. Does the minister not agree with that?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Actually, I believe we are going to have both, because the personnel in the Department of Reconstruction and1 Supply, who have had those contacts with industry, which the hon. member considers of considerable value, are to be transferred to the Canadian Commercial Corporation for the express purpose of maintaining the continuity to which he has referred. But in addition, in the Department of National Defence itself, we are continuing the close contact with industry that we have had. Out view is that that is well in hand.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question along the lines of that asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South. What will be the position of our arsenals at Valcartier and Lindsay? Prior to the war, the house was told that those arsenals were to be used for some development of our own. During the war a great many manufacturing establishments throughout Canada were used to develop and produce machines for the manufacture of munitions. At the time I understood that the cost of production of those machines was paid by this country. Are either the pilot machines or the machines made for and at the request of the government to be stored in our own arsenals for any possible future
National Defence Act

emergency, so that they can be used as samples by manufacturers to get back into production again.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The hon. member has referred to the work done by Canadian Arsenals Limited during the war. That was a crown company which took over the work of the Canadian arsenals, as was carried on at Valcartier and Lindsay. This was greatly developed during the war and the work will be carried on. At the present time it is reporting through the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Whether or not it will continue to be carried on in that department, or in some other department, must yet be determined. There is no doubt, however, as to our carrying on that work, not only with regard to the production of any munitions of war which might be needed in peace time, but also with regard to the development of pilot plant and applied research.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I had in mind one other matter along those lines. We had in Hamilton a large factory for the manufacture of guns. I am wondering if any of the equipment used to make the guns, which undoubtedly was paid for by the country, was stored in our arsenals, or if any sample machines were stored there to be used in any future emergency.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I think the answer is that almost all the machine tools, which we added enormously to during the war, were tools capable of peacetime uses. As we ended war production, those tools were disposed of through War Assets Corporation for use in civilian industry and if it were necessary the process could be reversed and the tools once used in war could be used again in war.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Are Canadian Arsenals not
to be under the Department of National Defence? We have been told that the Department of Reconstruction and Supply is to give up this job of purchasing for defence departments. Which department is to be eventually in charge of Canadian Arsenals?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
That has not been finally determined. My view is that the Department of National Defence should have just as little to do with purely civilian activities such as production and so on as is possible. We should limit ourselves to defence activities as such. I am really thinking out loud now. It may be that Canadian Arsenals will come back to the Department of National Defence and, if so, we shall welcome them. It may go to some other department if reconstruction and supply closes down. Possibly Canadian Arsenals will come to defence and some of the

other activities such as purchasing will go to trade and commerce as well as some part of the inspection.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that the right of procurement for the Department of National Defence is not being retained and that other duties were being assigned to the Department of Trade and Commerce and to the Canadian Commercial Corporation. Is it not a fact that the personnel who were in the procurement branch of the Department of National Defence prior to the war and who were lent to munitions and supply, later reconstruction and supply, under the war supply board, are now being invited1 to join the Canadian Commercial Corporation and are being faced with the fact that their former positions in the procurement branch of national defence are abolished?
Such being the case, is it not a fact that national defence is to be entirely deprived of all connections with procurement, even to the extent of abandoning the personnel that have been built up, and that Canadian Commercial Corporation, a crown company, is to procure supplies for the Department of National Defence along with its other duties? Is it not true that besides the career civil servants who were in the Department of National Defence and who were charged with the procurement of supplies, there are loanees from private industry who will be doing this work? That being the case, I think there is considerable weight to the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South that we should think well before the procurement of supplies and commodities is taken out of the Department of National Defence and given to a crown company.
Would the minister explain that situation? I believe that in procuring weapons and supplies for national defence it is much better to have it done through the department directly concerned than through a crown company which is much farther removed from responsibility to parliament and from the direct control of the Department of National Defence. In view of the fact that a statement has been made that this duty was being transferred out of his department, I think the minister should give us a statement on policy.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Vancouver South said, during the war the Department of Munitions and Supply developed very useful associations with industry. Our thought was that at the end of the war those associations should not be ended but that some branch of government should continue to have close contacts with indus-

National Defence Act
try, that could be used in the event of war. It seemed to us to be the most sensible course to transfer from the Department of Munitions and Supply some of the key personnel who had done so well during the war to an agency of government and so continue to make available in the public service information they had gained in the war. On that account the decision was taken and announced in the house on February 5, 1947, to have the functions of defence purchasing, hitherto exercised by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, transferred to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That seemed to be the sensible way to proceed and that is the way it was done.
The functions of the Department of National Defence with regard to procurement will be limited largely to special classes of things of which there is only one possible source, and even then they will work closely with the Canadian Commercial Corporation. If it is not done in that way it is possible that we may get into a situation which my hon. friends would be the first to refer to as giving an opportunity for what they would call political patronage and the like. What has been done seemed to us to be the most effective way of ensuring that the job is efficiently done, that it is done having regard to the interests of the defence of Canada and also to make sure that our war-won experience and knowledge and skill continues to be made available in the national interest.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
The minister says that
if it were left with the Department of National Defence it would be subject to political patronage.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: 1 did not say anything of the kind.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Does the minister not
realize that in a crown company set up with loanees from private industry, many of whom may be particularly interested in the things they are purchasing, more interested in their regular vocation than in their temporary employment, a company which is acting apart from the Civil Service Act, apart from immediate responsibility to government, utterly divorced from parliament, there is much greater advantage for political patronage of favouritism? The opportunities for this sort of thing would be much greater than the patronage that might emanate from members of parliament. The patronage that might emanate from the key officers of the company would be of a much greater degree than that which would occur in any department administered by permanent career civil servants.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say that it was his intention or desire that arsenals should be removed from the Department of National Defence.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
No. I said that as a
general idea it was my view that it would be a good thing for the Department of National Defence to relieve itself of all functions other than those having to do with pure defence. That would not necessarily include Arsenals.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity to give this matter sufficient thought to be absolutely sure that I am right; but, as the Minister of Veterans Affairs will remember, we had some worrisome days before the war over this question of equipment. At the outbreak of the war we found ourselves in a terrible position. I hope the government has not finally decided that this move is to go through. I understood that it was only the purchasing of supplies for defence purposes that was to be turned over to the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
But when I read the Prime Minister's statement, at page 132 of Hansard, I find that he said: "to buy or produce war supplies and to carry out projects required by the Department of National Defence." All the rest of. his statement refers only to purchasing. The Prime Minister points out that this Canadian Commercial Corporation is a purchasing agency, which is correct. But when we go from purchasing to producing we move into an entirely different field. Production, of course, was the main field of the Department of Reconstruction. Surely the Canadian Commercial Corporation will not be sufficiently interested in the procuring of equipment for the defence of this country to make a specialty of planning for the production of war materials. Certainly the Department of Trade and Commerce will not be interested to anything like the same degree as the Department of National Defence. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is sitting here right now and I am sure that he would agree with me. It is not the job of his department to make plans for being in a position to produce the weapons of war when they are needed. That surely is part of the job of the defence department. The job of the defence department has been too limited by the minister tonight. He says that they just have to do with the defence of the country. But we know from our experience in the years before the war that one of the main jobs of the defence department was to get Canada in a position to produce war
National Defence Act

equipment. I urge the minister to give further consideration to my suggestion that cooperation with industry and the actual production problems having to do with war equipment be handled by the Department of National Defence. Let the Canadian Commercial Corporation under the Department of Trade and Commerce do the actual buying, but do not make them responsible for seeing that this country is in a position to produce what weapons are required.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I made it very clear that cooperation with industry was being regarded by the Department of National Defence as an important part of its functions, and that is being seen to. With regard to the functions of the Department of Trade and Commerce in defence matters, the only thing that has been transferred is purchasing. The other matters, the ultimate disposition of Canadian Arsenals and the like, are quite open. We shall certainly give consideration to the views that have been expressed.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Then the Prime Minister when he spoke of the Canadian Commercial Corporation being responsible for producing war supplies and carrying out projects required by the defence department went farther than was the intention of the government. Is that, correct?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The corporation would have power to do that but it has not yet been entrusted with any opportunity to exercise that power. That is open for consideration.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Defence research board.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
There are two questions I wish to raise on this section. I have occasionally been twitted in the house for not having legal training. I have listened to a lot of lawyers talking this afternoon. I want to get some cheap legal advice and I know of no better way of getting it than by raising this question here. Subsection 4 of the new section 5, appearing on page 1 of the bill, provides:
Such officers, clerks and employees as are necessary for carrying on the business of the department may be appointed in the manner authorized by law.
Then subsection 4 of the new section 8, appearing on page 2 of the bill, provides:
The governor in council may by regulation:-
(a) notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act and section five of this act prescribe the manner of selection-

-of the staff of the defence research board. Does that mean that the governor in council can disregard the law in making these appointments?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The governor in council can go outside the law in making these appointments?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Outside the Civil Service Act.	.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Subsection 4 of the new section 8 mentions the Civil Service Act, but subsection 4 of the new section 5 simply says that such officers and employees as are necessary may be appointed in the manner authorized by law.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: There is only one law applicable I think, and that is the Civil Service Act.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Then I think it might be well to have said so, in order not to confuse those who are not lawyers.
I have another question. Subsection 3 of the new section 8 provides that the defence research board may:
(a) enter into contracts in the name of His Majesty and establish scholarships in connection with and make grants in aid for research and investigations for national defence.
Is it intended that the results of all the work of the defence research board shall be applicable only to defence projects, or will they be made available for the benefit of productive enterprise throughout the country?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Anything with civilian application will be made available.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Subsection 5 of the new section 8 says:
The minister may request the Minister of Finance to allocate any portion of the moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose of the board for scholarships or grants in aid of research.
Why is it necessary to have that sentence in at all? It would seem to me that, if the moneys are voted in a general appropriation for the purpose of defence research, there would be no necessity for this procedure of requesting the Minister of Finance to allocate any portion of the moneys, whereas if the moneys were specifically appropriated to a certain defence research project this section would give the minister power to divert the moneys appropriated by parliament for a specific purpose to some other purpose. It would appear to me that the moneys will either be voted by parliament in a general

National Defence Act
appropriation to be used for general purposes or in a specific appropriation when it would be the intention of parliament that the moneys were not to be switched from one purpose to another.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The only purpose of this sentence is this. Say' that the defence research board have a man who is doing a good job of research in a university which will have defence usefulness and that they want him to continue on that job for two years. They get from parliament a certain sum of money in their vote for defence research. Then they can go to the Minister of Finance and get him to allocate that money if more than one year is required to enable that man to complete his job.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: This is just so that it will not lapse?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: That is the only purpose.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
What do these words in subsection 5 of section 8 mean?
All expenses of the defence research board shall be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the purpose or received by the board through the conduct of its operation, bequests, donations or otherwise.
I take it that this defence research board will engage in some operations through which it will itself make money. Appropriations and bequests will be made, but only in the case of specific appropriations will parliament be authorized to pass upon any of the expenditures. Will the minister explain it?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I understand that this provision is taken from the provisions of the National Research Council Act, and while I do not expect that many people will donate money for the purpose of defence research, it is possible that, as a by-product of defence research, the board may receive in Canada or from outside Canada money which could be used again.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I might point out to the minister that, under the National Research Council Act, the national research council is authorized not only to do research but to carry on manufacturing, to sell its products, to sell patents, to sell inventions and to get considerable revenue. When passing the National Research Council Act last year many hon. members were quite alarmed at the fact that the national research council could get in its own money and invest it without its being appropriated by parliament at all. We are now giving to the research defence board the same privilege, under which they will be making profits, possibly and spending their profits
without any accounting to parliament whatever and not even to the Minister of National Defence. The fact that this section is in the National Research Council Act is no justification whatever for its being in this bill. Unless it is contemplated that the defence research board is to make money other than through receiving bequests and obtaining money other than from parliament, this section should not be in the bill. If it does get money, then it should deposit it in the consolidated revenue fund and have it appropriated for specific purposes. It is not good business for parliament to delegate power of this kind, power to spend money which may have been earned, without accounting to parliament for it.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The hon. member will appreciate that in this matter we shall very likely be cooperating frequently with other nations, and it is possible that just as we might join in a joint project with some other country to develop something of common interest to us, and might contribute to its expenses, so we might expect them to contribute to the expenses of doing a job of research in our country. In that event they would want to have the money they contributed go directly to the job of research. That is about the only kind of situation that we can envisage which is likely to arise in this matter. I think it is worth while to keep the power in the bill.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
If the minister will reflect on it I think he will find that the section goes a little farther than that.
There are other points in the section to which I should like to raise objection. Subsection 2 of old section 8 says:
The director general of defence research and the other members of the board shall hold office during pleasure and shall be paid such salaries, remuneration and expenses as may be fixed from time to time by the governor in council.
This is an important body. Altogether too much leeway is being given to it to change from time to time the salary, remuneration and terms of employment not only of the officials but of the employees of the defence research board. Subsection 4, paragraph (a) reads:
notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act and section 5 of this act, prescribe the manner of selection, remuneration and terms of appointment and service of the officers and employees engaged in the work of the defence research board . . .
It seems to me that the government is definitely going out of its way to free itself from any possible connection with the Civil Service Act. I believe that the employees and
National Defence Act

many of the officials of the defence research board stand in exactly the same position as men in any department of government who are given employment under the Civil Service Act. The paragraph to which I have just referred goes farther and says:
(3) Subject to the approval of the governor in council, the defence research board may,
(b) establish and support a pension fund or make other pension or superannuation arrangements for the benefit of all or any of the permanent or temporary officers or employees of the defence research board.
If this board, as the minister would lead us to believe, and as he said the other day, sought to come under the same pension scheme as the national research council there might be some little justification for that, but this paragraph gives them the power to set up their own pension scheme, to regulate their own terms of employment in so far as temporaries and permanents are concerned. It is possible that they will have many men on loan from private industry working side by side with men who are on loan from one of the departments of government, men who are permanent employees under the Civil Service Act. If men from private industry on loan to the defence research board were given the same superannuation that they had in private or that provided under the Civil Service Superannuation Act I do not see that there could be very great objection to their paying contributions while they were there, but this is entirely different. This section says that not only shall we pay them salaries, not only shall they have power to make provision to continue the superannuation that they had when they came to us from private industry or from another department of government, but we are setting up a separate and distinct superannuation scheme. In addition to that, I do not think we are playing fair with the civil servants who have entered the profession to make it a career when we allow men from the defence research board1 to dictate to us and set up for their employees a scheme or an arrangement different from or better than that under the Civil Service Act. If the Civil Service Superannuation Act is good enough for the permanent career civil servants, surely it should be good1 enough for those who come to the defence research board on loan from private industry.
This section goes a great deal farther than that. I say this with the utmost sincerity. If the minister will look at this I think he will find that it will cause a great deal of dissatisfaction, a great deal of jealousy and a great deal of animosity among the permanent civil servants, the men who have entered' the

service of their country and have made it a career. I would ask the minister to think this matter over carefully. I believe we are giving the defence research board, with the approval of the cabinet, something that should be handled by parliament itself, something that should be handled by the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Superannuation Act.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
May I reply quickly. The hon. member has referred to section 8 (2) of the act as it would be amended. There is no suggestion that anyone should receive any salary to be fixed by that section except the members of the board and the director general. As the hon. member knows, deputy ministers and the like have their salaries fixed by the governor in council.
With regard to the question of pensions, the intention is that the permanent staff will come under the Civil Service Superannuation Act; the scientific staff will come under the national research council pension fund, if one is established. If a couple of years go by and there is no such fund1, then some measure would have to be found to look after the scientists. I should point out that as regards the scientific personnel of the defence research board, it is not expected that they will be employed over very long periods of time. It is expected that they will have to go back to their universities, their institutions or their industries. They will be here for limited periods of time. They will have to receive salaries that are fixed accordingly and will work usually in difficult circumstances and in rather uncomfortable places, involving a considerable amount of risk without any possibility of public acclaim or praise. On that account it is not possible to fit them into the ordinary civil service structure. With regard to the ordinary employees, they will be dealt with along the ordinary lines and it is felt that there is no difficulty there. I believe that this measure meets the need for the creation of a defence research board, and if the board can be established on a sound foundation in the next year we shall probably find it desirable to give it a more permanent structure in the form of some special act. But at the present time it is considered that this is the most flexible way in which to deal with an urgent problem; that is, to continue the good work done by the highly skilled people who have been working for us during the war, and this we believe to be the best way to do it.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Does the minister not agree that such employees as are not specially skilled or scientific should be left under the Civil Service Act and the superannuation act? There are many of those who fit into exactly

Housing
the same classifications as men under the Civil Service Act. Surely they should be left under that act.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
There will not be very
many employees of that class except daily-rate employees. This does not envisage a large-scale organization.
